items.title: About
items.text:
EasyDiffraction models and fits diffraction data. Build a structural model, compare its calculated pattern with your measurements, fit the parameters you choose and save everything as one project.

Use it in your browser, on your desktop, from Python or from the command line. All of them open the same projects.

items.title: Where to start
items.text:
• User guide: the ideas and the analysis workflow.
  • Application, Python Python and Command line: how to work in each one.
  • Physics: the models and equations behind the calculations.

items.title: How to cite
items.text: If you use EasyDiffraction in your work, please cite it. The app shows the same citation under Home → How to cite.

items.title: Citation
items.text:
Sazonov, A. (2026). EasyDiffraction [Computer software]. DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22905049

@software{easydiffraction,
  author = {Sazonov, Andrew},
  title = {EasyDiffraction},
  year = {2026},
  doi = {10.5281/zenodo.22905049},
  url = {https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22905049}
}

Zenodo keeps a record of every release under that DOI. The app's How to cite adds the version and year of the build you run.

Also say which version of EasyDiffraction you used. The app shows it in its About window, and in Python edi.__version__ holds it.

items.title: Keep your analysis repeatable
items.text:
Save the project with your result. It holds the data, the structural model and every setting, so you or someone else can open it and continue. A report gives a readable summary of the model and the fit; keep it alongside the project.

Also cite the sources of your data and structural models.

items.title: Get in touch
items.text: Ask a question, share feedback, report a problem or suggest an idea. Messages reach the same people as the app's Help and feedback.

items.title: Send a message
items.text:
When you report a problem, it helps to say:

  • what you did, what happened and what you expected;
  • whether you use the browser app, the desktop app, Python or the command line, and its version;
  • a small project or file that shows the problem, if you can share it. Leave out unpublished or confidential data.
Send

items.title: Take the survey
items.text: Have 15 minutes? The survey asks how you work and what you need, and it shapes what we build next.

items.title: Other ways
items.text: You can also open an issue on GitHub. If you would like to work on the code, its source is in the edi repository.

items.title: Licence
items.text:
EasyDiffraction is open source.

  • Source code: BSD 3-Clause License.
  • Desktop and browser app: GNU General Public License version 3.

The source is on GitHub. Libraries and data it uses keep their own licences.

The coloured status icons in this documentation are Twemoji graphics by Twitter, Inc. and other contributors, used unchanged under CC BY 4.0.

items.title: Survey
items.text:
Tell us how you analyse diffraction data and what you need from EasyDiffraction. It takes about 15 minutes, every question is optional, and you can send it at any time. If you are at a workshop or another event, choose it under Event so we can see the answers from that event together.

Your answers are anonymous unless you give your name, e-mail or affiliation at the end. They go to the EasyDiffraction developers only.

items.title: Install and update
items.text:
EasyDiffraction comes with all required application dependencies. Download and extract the whole ZIP for your platform. The online installer needs an internet connection. The installers are not signed yet: on macOS, open the installer once, then select Open Anyway in System Settings → Privacy & Security.

macOSWindowsLinux
  1. Open the extracted installer app.
  2. If macOS blocks it, click Done. In System Settings → Privacy & Security, scroll to Security, select Open Anyway, and confirm. This applies to the installer you just opened. Apple’s instructions
  3. Follow setup. The suggested folder is /Applications/EasyDiffraction.
  1. Right-click the ZIP and select Extract All, then open the installer .exe.
  2. If Microsoft Defender SmartScreen warns about the installer, use More info → Run anyway if Windows offers it and you downloaded the installer using the links above. Smart App Control can block unsigned apps without offering a per-app exception. Microsoft’s Smart App Control guide
  3. Follow setup to choose the installation folder.
  1. Keep the extracted .run file beside the installer-runtime folder.

  2. In a terminal opened in that folder, make the installer executable and run it.

    chmod +x ./EasyDiffraction-*-linux-x86_64-online.run
./EasyDiffraction-*-linux-x86_64-online.run

  3. Follow setup to choose the installation folder.

EasyDiffraction checks for updates at startup and hourly while it is open. To check on demand, open Preferences → Updates and select Check now.

When a newer release is available, select the red Update button at the bottom left to review the release notes and start the update. Notify about updates also opens the notes automatically when a new version is found. The updater installs into your existing location. On the next launch, What's new shows the changes since your previous version.

items.title: Open local projects
items.text:
Choose Open project… and select a folder or zip archive. You can also drop a project folder, its project.edi file or a zip archive onto the application window.

An archive opens as a temporary working copy. Save updates the archive when it is writable; otherwise the app asks where to save it.

items.title: Save and share
items.text:
Save project as… writes a folder or zip archive. Select Save a copy to write to another location while continuing in the original project.

Use a folder to access individual model and result files, or a zip archive to move the complete project. Reports are saved in the project's reports/ folder, inside the archive when the project is a zip. When the project cannot be written back, such as an example or a read-only archive, the app first asks where to save it.

The application layout and example fit apply to both desktop and web versions.

items.title: Analysis
items.text:
Fitting adjusts the parameters you choose to bring the calculated result closer to the measured data. Begin with a structural model and experiment that plausibly describe the measurement; fitting is not a substitute for checking those choices.

The shared Analysis chapter explains the scientific model; the steps below describe this interface.

items.text:
Look at peak positions, widths, intensities and the background before fitting. An incorrect wavelength or calibration can shift peaks; a missing phase can leave intensity the model cannot explain.

items.title: Choose free parameters
items.text:
On Analysis, the parameter table lists every numerical input of the structures and experiments. Use the free column to choose which parameters may vary. When a fit cannot vary a value, its checkbox is disabled and hovering over it shows the reason. The name and variability filters help you find them.

A value cannot be fitted when it describes the setup, symmetry or a constraint sets it, the fit's data cannot determine it, or the calculation has no derivative for it yet. A value saved as free that cannot be fitted opens as fixed, and Messages says so. The minimum and maximum displayed in the table describe admissible model values; they are not a separate set of user-defined optimizer bounds.

Free parameters deliberately, checking the effect of each stage. Starting with every parameter free can hide an unsuitable model behind strongly correlated values.

items.title: Start and inspect the fit
items.text:
Press Fit at the right of the status bar. Review the calculated curve and residual as well as the reported agreement factors. Parameter uncertainties and correlations help you understand what the data constrain.

A small agreement factor alone does not establish that the structural model is correct. Inspect unmodelled features and physically implausible values before accepting the result.

items.title:  Fitting mode
items.text:
pd sc cwl tof neut xray Fitting

Shown: with measured data.

The fitting mode determines how the project's experiments or scan datasets are fitted. It changes the relationship between fits, not the meaning of the structures and experiments.

The shared fitting-mode guide explains single, joint, sequential and independent fitting, including their starting-state policies. This page explains the application controls.

items.title: Select the mode in the app
items.text:
Open Analysis and use the fitting-mode control. The choices reflect the project: with only one applicable mode the selector is disabled and explains why.

A joint fit shows the experiment weights. A scan mode shows its scan declaration. The mode is saved as part of the project and is also read by Python and Command line analysis.

The available choices depend on the project.

Fitting mode

items.title: Fit a scan
items.text:
Use sequential when each result should seed the next fit, or independent when you want each dataset to start from the same template. Follow the scan guide for dataset selection, progress, continuation and evolution charts.

Choose sequential, independent or single-dataset fitting.

Fitting mode

items.title: Fit the shown scan dataset on its own
items.text:
A scan can use single to fit the shown dataset. That result becomes the template, and the selected file becomes the template dataset. Check the template before starting a full scan.

items.title: Fit several experiments jointly
items.text:
This example is pd-neut-xray-cwl_pbso4-d1a-lab: PbSO₄ [Pnma], D1A @ ILL and laboratory X-ray.

A joint fit uses all the project's experiments together. Shared structural parameters can be informed by more than one measurement, while each experiment keeps its own instrument, background and other settings.

Review the experiment weights and linked structures before running. A joint result should still be inspected experiment by experiment.

Follow these stages in the application. Each one has its own page in the top bar of the workspace.

  1. Project
  2. Structure
  3. Experiment
  4. Analysis
  5. Report
Stage In Application Project Create a project, then open and save your work Structure Load a structure and edit its symmetry, cell and atom sites Experiment Add data and set the instrument, peak profile and background Analysis Fit a pattern and inspect the fit Report Review the result and save the report

The shared analysis workflow explains the science behind each stage.

items.title: Estimation settings
items.text:
The Extra tab's Background group holds the estimation settings. It appears once the experiment has measured data. Leave a field empty to let the estimator choose where that option supports automatic selection.

Setting Purpose Calculated peaks Use auto, subtract the model's calculated peaks, or ignore them. Anchor points Control the number of points in a line-segment background. Max terms Limit the number of polynomial or Chebyshev terms. Baseline method Select the method used to find the curve under the peaks. Peak width and smoothness Control the scale on which the baseline is estimated. Noise tolerance Control how closely the points or terms follow the estimated curve.

Subtracting calculated peaks can help where peaks overlap and the measured intensity never reaches the background. A poor model can make subtraction misleading. The default auto choice checks whether the model is suitable and reports its choice below the settings.

Inspect background estimation settings.

items.title: Choose a background representation
items.text:
The application supports line-segment backgrounds, represented by points, and polynomial or Chebyshev backgrounds, represented by terms. The Background group shows the values for the current experiment.

Changing the background type replaces its representation; review the confirmation before removing points or terms you want to keep.

items.title: Estimate the background
items.text:
On Experiment, choose Estimate in the Background group. The estimate replaces the current points or terms. Undo brings the previous values back. Estimate needs measured data: until data are loaded into the experiment, the button is disabled and its tooltip says why.

The estimation mode controls what happens next:

  • Manual keeps the current values for editing. Estimate runs when you ask for it.
  • Auto estimates again when the measured data or estimation settings change. The table shows the estimated values; choose manual to edit them.

You can still free or fix a value through its context menu.

items.title: A practical sequence
items.text:
1. Load the data and estimate the background while the model is still rough.
  2. Fit the structure and profile, keeping the background fixed or freeing selected background values.
  3. Inspect the residual and estimate again if the improved model makes the background clearer.

items.text:
Select an experiment on Experiment → Main, then expand Instrument. Enter the measurement conditions in the units shown. The available fields depend on the experiment type: constant-wavelength measurements use a wavelength; time-of-flight measurements use calibration coefficients.

Facility and Instrument record where the measurement was made. After you load a data file into an experiment, choose each from its list. Otherwise they show what the saved or loaded experiment states. Check the numerical settings against the measurement before fitting peak positions.

items.title: Project
items.text:
Use the application to open, save and export the complete analysis. The shared Project stage explains what belongs in a project; data formats explains its folder and archive representations.

Saving in the browser

Check the project location before closing the app. In this browser only means the project is in browser storage; use Save project as… to keep an external copy. Browser-specific saving explains folders, archives and downloads.

items.title: What is saved
items.text:
Saving writes the project state and measured data, including the selected analysis settings. Values are rounded according to the project's precision and uncertainty policy. The open project is updated to those saved values and its calculated pattern and agreement factors are recalculated from them.

A report is separate: saving a project does not create a fresh report. Use Save report to update a document you intend to share.

A project can read measured data from files outside its folder. On Project → Extra, expand Data on save to choose what a save does with them: copy every file into the project, keep linked files linked, or ask on every save. The choice is kept for this project's folder. Until you choose, a save copies the data when it is small (up to 20 files and 50 MB) and keeps larger data linked.

items.title: Save or save a copy
items.text:
Save writes to the project's current location when that is writable. Save project as… lets you choose a different location or format.

On the desktop, Save project as… offers Folder, Zip archive, and Save a copy. A copy records the current state without moving the project you continue to work on.

An archive opened on the desktop is unpacked into a working copy. Save writes the archive again. If it is not writable, or it is a bundled example, the application asks where to keep your work instead.

items.title: Save the report
items.text:
Select the desired formats in Export, then choose Save report. The files are written to the project's reports/ folder, inside the zip when the project is a zip archive. An example or a read-only archive cannot be written back, so the desktop app first asks where to save the project, then saves the report there. The web app also downloads the report files, as one file or one zip of them.

Turning off a format leaves any previously saved file in place; it does not delete it.

items.text:

items.title: Fit with the AI assistant
items.text: The app has an AI assistant built in. Give it a structure and a measured pattern and ask it to fit the structure: it asks for what the files do not say, then sets up the project and fits it in stages, as the tutorials do by hand. This page follows one run on La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ measured on HRPT, the case of the La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ on HRPT tutorial.

items.title: Get the two files
items.text:
Download them from EasyDiffraction's collection:

  • tutorial-lbco.cif: the structure.
  • tutorial-hrpt.xye: the measured pattern.

items.title: Open and connect
items.text:
The assistant needs the desktop app and a ChatGPT account (see AI assistant). Open it with the robot button in the toolbar and connect.

PanelConnect

Open the assistant from the toolbar

Connect ChatGPT

items.text:
With Show actions on, the app shows each action the assistant takes as it works, on the control it uses. This run leaves it off, so the assistant works in the background and reports in the chat.

The assistant is connected; Show actions is off

items.text:
Attach both files with the + button, ask it to fit the crystal structure, and send. The app asks before it shares the project and the files.

items.title: Answer its question
items.text:
The pattern does not say which radiation or wavelength was used, so the assistant asks. Answer, and it fits the structure.

QuestionFittedPattern

The assistant asks what the files do not say

Answer, and the assistant fits the structure

The fitted pattern on Analysis

items.title: What it did
items.text: It asked whether the data were neutron or X-ray and for the wavelength, built the project from the two files, fitted in stages and shared one displacement between La and Ba. It ended at a = 3.890787(37) Å, within the tutorial's result, with La/Ba B iso 0.410(34) Å² against the tutorial's 0.55(6) Å², Rwp 6.91 % and reduced χ² 1.19, freeing 32 parameters where the tutorial frees 15. Its last step, saving the project, returned no confirmation. Tried with gpt-6.1-sol on 2026-11-09; another run can take other steps, so check the result against the La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ on HRPT tutorial.

items.text:

items.text:

items.text:

items.title: Constrain the two Co sites
items.text:
The correlations show no strong pair for the two Co sites, yet the fit gives them very different displacements, Co1's even negative, which no atom can have: both are Co and scatter alike, so the pattern cannot tell their thermal motions apart. Give each an alias and constrain Co2's to follow Co1's, starting again from 0.5 Å², then fit again; the shared displacement is positive and its s.u. smaller than either had alone.

Filter the Atomic displacement parameters with [Co2] in their name using the category filter and the name filter, click the Free column header and choose Fixed · all, then press Fit in the status bar.

Fit: Constrain the two Co sites

items.title: Oxygen occupancies
items.text:

items.title: Run, stop and continue
items.text:
Press Fit at the right of the status bar, on any page, and follow the dataset counts beside it. While a run is under way the button reads Stop; stopping keeps the completed results. It then reads Continue, which resumes from the first unfitted file, or Refit after a change to the template, which fits every file again. Reset, next to it, clears every dataset's result for another run, and Undo restores the preceding results.

Follow, also in the status bar, displays the dataset currently being fitted. Selecting another dataset turns it off; select Follow again to follow progress. Display and updates controls redraw frequency.

Read project counts, messages, calculation and fitting state here.

items.title: Inspect the scan views
items.text:
Use Stacked to compare the patterns one above another or Map to inspect intensity across the series as rows of colour. On Stacked, Spacing runs from Overlay, every pattern on one baseline, through Close, Medium and Wide, the default, to Separate, each pattern in its own band. Its legend, turned on from the toolbar, lists the files; click an entry to hide that pattern. On Map, choose the colour map, Blue-Red by default or Viridis, Batlow, Inferno, Lapaz or Greys, and its Direction: Auto, Normal or Inverted. Subtract background draws each pattern less the project's background, here and on the pattern chart. Evolution plots a fitted parameter with its uncertainty against a selected dataset value or its place in the scan. Select a point to inspect that dataset elsewhere in the app.

Correlations shows the selected dataset's last fit. Only the template dataset's correlations are retained when saving and reopening the project. After editing the template, earlier results remain visible but are marked out of date until refitted.

items.title: Scale, 2θ zero and cell
items.text:
The scale sets the overall height of the pattern, and the zero shift and the cell length put the peaks where they are measured, so they come first.

A group is freed in one action: choose it in the category filter above the table, then click the Free column header and choose Free · all.

FilterFree · all

Filter the table to Background

Free all from the Free column header

Filter the Linked structures and Cell parameters, one category at a time, using the category filter and the Instrument parameters with calib in their name using the category filter and the name filter, click the Free column header and choose Free · all, then press Fit in the status bar.

items.title: Background
items.text:
With the peaks in place, the five background points follow the level between them.

Filter the Background parameters using the category filter, click the Free column header and choose Free · all, then press Fit in the status bar.

Fit: Background

items.title: Peak widths
items.text:
The profile terms now fit the widths and shapes of the peaks.

Filter the Peak profile parameters using the category filter, click the Free column header and choose Free · all; then type lorentz_x in the name filter and choose Fixed · all in the same menu, then press Fit in the status bar.

Fit: Peak widths

items.title: Displacements
items.text:
Every atom sits on a special position of P m -3 m, so there are no coordinates to fit. The displacements change the peak intensities with angle and come last.

Filter the Atomic displacement parameters using the category filter, click the Free column header and choose Free · all, then press Fit in the status bar.

Fit: Displacements

items.title: Constrain La and Ba
items.text:
The correlations show the displacements of La and Ba moving together almost exactly, with opposite signs: they share one site and scatter neutrons similarly, so the pattern cannot tell them apart, and their s.u. are large. Give each an alias and constrain Ba's to follow La's, then fit again. Ba's displacement is no longer fitted on its own.

Filter the Atomic displacement parameters with [Ba] in their name using the category filter and the name filter, click the Free column header and choose Fixed · all, then press Fit in the status bar.

Fit: Constrain La and Ba

items.title: Start here
items.text: Run saved projects from a terminal or a shell script.

items.title: Choose an installation
items.text:
Standalone executablePython Python package

Download the executable for your operating system and run edi …. No Python is needed. It fits projects with edi fit.

Download the standalone executable

Install edi in a Python environment and run python -m edi …. Besides fitting, it calculates patterns, exports, undoes, manages collections, writes reports and shows live fit progress.

Set up the Python package's command line

items.title: What a run looks like
items.text:
EasyDiffraction command-line session

The guides show each command for both installations; pick the tab that matches yours.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Run an example.
  • Look up a command in the command reference.

items.title: Repeat an analysis
items.text: Use ordinary shell or workflow tools to run several complete projects. There is no additional batch command to learn: each project declares the model and analysis it needs.

items.title: Separate output folders
items.text:
For a shell with the input folders projects/sample-a and projects/sample-b:

Standalone executablePython package 
set -e
mkdir -p logs runs

for project in projects/sample-a projects/sample-b; do
    case_name=$(basename "$project")
    edi fit "$project" \
        --output "runs/$case_name" \
        --report machine \
        > "logs/$case_name.txt" \
        2> "logs/$case_name-errors.txt"
done

set -e
mkdir -p logs runs

for project in projects/sample-a projects/sample-b; do
    case_name=$(basename "$project")
    python -m edi fit "$project" \
        --output "runs/$case_name" \
        --report machine \
        > "logs/$case_name.txt" \
        2> "logs/$case_name-errors.txt"
done

This loop is a shell example, not a new edi API. It stops on a failed command and keeps reports separate from project output. Give each input a distinct output name and retain its original files.

items.title: Run without keeping model changes
items.text: Add --dry to execute fits without writing project changes. A dry run does real numerical work. In scan mode it keeps no resumable progress, so use an ordinary output folder for a scan you intend to continue.

items.title: A scan is a project workflow
items.text:
If the measured files belong to one sequential or independent scan, declare that scan in the project instead of treating every pattern as an unrelated batch project.

  • Sequential: the previous fit supplies the next pattern's initial parameters.
  • Independent: every pattern starts from the same initial parameters.

Both process files serially. See shared fitting modes.

items.title: Keep failure information
items.text: Check the process exit status and retain stderr. A machine report is a versioned record; scripts that parse it should handle its schema and failed-run records explicitly. Do not treat the existence of a redirected output file as proof of a successful fit.

items.title: Save reports after fitting
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report runs/sample-a
python -m edi report runs/sample-a --check

Use the report guide to choose contents and check freshness.

items.title: Calculate a project
items.text: calc predicts the data from the current model. It does not optimize parameters, and it can run a complete simulation project without measured observations.

items.title: Run a calculation
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no calc; use the Python package.

python -m edi calc path/to/project

The project's structures, experiments, data grids and calculation settings supply the inputs. For powder data, the command writes calculated series into the experiment files, replacing the previous generated calculated block while preserving the measured columns. Reflection data is saved through the corresponding project model.

items.title: Calculate without writing
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no calc; use the Python package.

python -m edi calc path/to/project --dry

The calculation still runs and reports its result. The project's files stay unchanged. This is useful when inspecting a saved model without replacing its calculated series.

items.title: Keep a separate result
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no calc; use the Python package.

python -m edi calc path/to/project --output calculated-project
python -m edi calc project.zip --output calculated-project

A zip input is never rewritten by the calculation command. Without --output, it runs without retaining its changes and warns accordingly. Files and output describes the input forms.

items.title: Select the report channel
items.text:
Unlike fit, calc defaults to machine output. Ask for a readable summary with:

Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no calc; use the Python package.

python -m edi calc path/to/project --report human --dry

--verbosity off suppresses the report. For calculation, compact and full carry the same detail because there are no fit iterations or fitted-parameter table.

items.title: Prepare a document
items.text: After keeping the calculated project, use the report command to save an HTML report. Calculating a project and rendering its report are separate actions.

items.title: Get data and tutorials
items.text:
Both command lines list EasyDiffraction's collection and download from it, the same collection the application's Load ▾ From web… reads. The commands are the same with edi (the standalone executable) and python -m edi.

Standalone executablePython package 
edi list-data
edi list-data --kind project
edi download-data pd-neut-cwl_lbco-hrpt -d data
edi list-tutorials
edi download-tutorial pd-neut-cwl_lbco-hrpt -d tutorials
edi download-tutorial 1 --py
edi download-all-tutorials -d tutorials

python -m edi list-data
python -m edi list-data --kind project
python -m edi download-data pd-neut-cwl_lbco-hrpt -d data
python -m edi list-tutorials
python -m edi download-tutorial pd-neut-cwl_lbco-hrpt -d tutorials
python -m edi download-tutorial 1 --py
python -m edi download-all-tutorials -d tutorials

A name is an entry's id or its number in the listing; use the id in scripts. A project archive is unpacked into its own folder, and the command prints where. Sizes and SHA-256 digests are checked, and -o/--overwrite replaces what is already there. --source reads another collection; so does EDI_COLLECTION.

The standalone executable uses the operating system's secure connections: built in on Windows and macOS, and the libcurl library on Linux, which most systems have. Without it, the download commands say so, and --source with a local folder still works.

items.title: Experiments in a saved project
items.text: The saved experiment supplies measured data or a calculation range, instrument settings, peak profile, background, exclusions and links to structures. Commands use these settings when loading the complete project.

items.title: Prepare the experiment
items.text:
Use the application experiment controls or Python experiment objects to import observations and configure the experiment, then save the project.

The command line operates on that saved experiment. It does not create an experiment from a raw pattern file or offer a second set of instrument and background options on the fit command.

items.title: Choose the run
items.text:
• Calculate evaluates the model, including experiments with simulation ranges.
  • Fit uses measured observations and the fitting mode saved in the project.

Use --dry when you want to calculate or fit without writing project changes. It still executes the calculation or fit.

The shared Experiment stage explains the model, and fitting modes explains single, joint and scan analyses.

items.title: Files and output
items.text: The same complete project is used by the application, Python and Command line. Commands make their output destination explicit so you can retain an initial model and its result separately.

items.title: Accepted project inputs
items.text:
fit and calc accept:

Standalone executablePython package 
edi fit path/to/project
edi fit path/to/project/project.edi
edi fit project.zip --output fitted-project

python -m edi fit path/to/project
python -m edi fit path/to/project/project.edi
python -m edi fit project.zip --output fitted-project

A folder holds project.edi, structures/, experiments/, analysis/ and reports/. Its entry file opens that complete folder. A zip packages the project files together.

structures/ and experiments/ can hold CIF files as well as .edi ones. When both lbco.edi and lbco.cif are there, the .edi file is read and the .cif one is named in a warning on stderr. Items a CIF gives that EasyDiffraction does not read are reported the same way. Writing results back saves every member as .edi. See CIF files.

items.title: Where results are written
items.text:
Input and options fit / calc behavior Folder or project.edi, no output flag Writes a successful result back to that folder. --output DIR Works from an output folder and keeps its results there. --dry Runs the computation without writing project changes. Zip, no --output Keeps the archive unchanged; warns that results are not written back. Zip with --output DIR Keeps the input archive unchanged and retains results in the folder.

--dry takes precedence over writing an output folder. For scans it also prevents retaining progress files.

The zip rule differs from Python: Project.save() can rewrite an archive opened in Python, whereas these two commands do not overwrite their input archive.

items.title: Export a project archive
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no export; use the Python package.

python -m edi export path/to/project --output shared-project.zip

The short spelling is -o. Export packages the project folder as last saved; it is not a fit or a substitute for saving in-memory Python edits. The archive can be opened by another edi interface.

items.title: Keep logs separate from project output
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi fit path/to/project --report machine > fit.txt 2> fit-errors.txt

python -m edi fit path/to/project --report machine > fit.txt 2> fit-errors.txt

The report channel goes to stdout. Warnings and errors go to stderr. Redirecting text output does not change where the project itself is saved.

items.title: Output precision
items.text: Saving rounds values to the persisted precision, then recalculates the model from the saved values. Compare a reopened project with that saved model, rather than assuming every in-memory floating-point digit is written unchanged.

items.title: Run a fit
items.text: The command line loads a complete project and runs the analysis its settings declare. Use it for a single pattern, joint experiments, or a scan.

items.title: Run the project
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi fit path/to/project

python -m edi fit path/to/project

For a folder or its project.edi, this command fits and saves the project back to that folder when the run succeeds. Keep the initial model separately when you want to compare it with the result.

items.title: Choose the output
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi fit path/to/project --output fitted-project
edi fit path/to/project --dry

python -m edi fit path/to/project --output fitted-project
python -m edi fit path/to/project --dry

--output DIR keeps the result in another folder. With the standalone executable, choose a new folder and use either --output or --dry. A dry run still performs the fit and leaves the input files unchanged. It keeps no scan progress.

For an archive:

Standalone executablePython package 
edi fit project.zip --output fitted-project

python -m edi fit project.zip --output fitted-project

Without an output folder, fit leaves the input archive unchanged and warns that the results are not written back. See files and output.

items.title: Inspect more detail
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi fit path/to/project --verbosity full

python -m edi fit path/to/project --verbosity full

Full output includes the fitted parameter table. The Python package's command line also reports per-bank agreement factors for a joint fit.

items.title: Follow progress
items.text:
Live progress is available in the Python package's command line. Its human channel reports progress during a single fit. A scan reports progress per measured file; full verbosity adds its iteration detail. To request live progress records on the machine channel for a single or joint fit:

Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no fit --stream; use the Python package.

python -m edi fit path/to/project --report machine --stream

Machine streaming is not emitted for scans, whose independent per-file iterations are a different progression.

items.title: Read machine output
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi fit path/to/project --report machine

python -m edi fit path/to/project --report machine

The machine report uses a versioned key=value record suitable for comparing runs.

The chosen report goes to standard output; warnings and errors go to standard error. Preserve both when you need a record of an unattended run.

items.title: Fitting mode and minimizer
items.text: The project declares single, joint, sequential or independent mode. Its _minimizer settings choose the descent strategy, tolerance and iteration budget. They are project data, not extra fit flags. See fitting modes.

items.title: Stop and resume
items.text: In the Python package's command line, Ctrl+C requests a clean cancellation. The command exits with status 130. A cancelled single or joint fit leaves the project unchanged; a scan retains completed file results so running the same command can resume. A dry run retains no scan progress. A second Ctrl+C terminates immediately.

items.title: Prepare a report
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report path/to/project
python -m edi report path/to/project --check

The first command writes the selected report formats except PDF. The second checks whether saved reports are current without writing them.

items.title: Continue visually
items.text: Open the saved project in the application. Its structures and experiments are the same ones the command line reads.

items.title: Command line from the Python package
items.text: The Python package includes the command-line interface. You do not need to write a Python script or use a notebook.

items.title: Install the package
items.text: Follow Python setup for the package and environment. The same installation provides both import edi and python -m edi.

items.title: Run a command
items.text:
Activate the environment containing the package, then check the command:

Standalone executablePython package 
edi --help

python -m edi --help

Pass a saved project directly:

Standalone executablePython package 
edi fit path/to/project --output fitted-project

python -m edi fit path/to/project --output fitted-project

The Python package's command line also provides calc, export, undo, collection, report and the data and tutorial downloads, plus live fit progress. Use Run a fit for the options, or Run an example to try a complete case.

items.title: Command reference
items.text:
The standalone executable supports fit. The Python package's command line supports fit, calc, report, export, undo, and collection. Use your installed version's help to see its options.

Standalone executablePython package 
edi --help
edi fit --help

python -m edi --help
python -m edi fit --help

items.title: Fit
items.text:
The standalone executable accepts:

edi fit PROJECT [--dry | --output DIRECTORY]
    [--verbosity off|compact|full] [--report human|machine]

The Python package's command line accepts:

python -m edi fit PROJECT [--output DIR] [--dry]
    [--verbosity off|compact|full] [--report human|machine] [--stream]

Default output is the human report at compact verbosity. A successful fit normally saves its folder. --dry executes without writing; a zip requires --output DIR to retain results. Full guide.

items.title: Calculate
items.text:
python -m edi calc PROJECT [--output DIR] [--dry]
    [--verbosity off|compact|full] [--report machine|human]

Default output is the machine report at compact verbosity. The project supplies its grid and model. Full guide.

items.title: Report
items.text:
python -m edi report PROJECT [--check] [--output PATH]
    [--offline|--online] [--x-axis native|d_spacing]
    [--correlation-threshold X] [--correlation-experiment NAME]
    [--exclude KEY ...|--include-all] [--colour-scheme NAME]

--check checks saved-report freshness without writing. --output PATH writes an HTML document instead of updating the saved-report list. Full guide.

items.title: Export
items.text:
python -m edi export PROJECT --output FILE.zip

-o is the short output spelling. This packages the project folder as last saved. Files and output.

items.title: Undo the last saved fit
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no undo; use the Python package.

python -m edi undo path/to/project --dry
python -m edi undo path/to/project --report human

The first command previews what would be restored. The second restores the persisted pre-fit state and saves it back when a snapshot exists. undo --dry is a preview, unlike fit --dry and calc --dry, which run their computations.

Undo supports --verbosity off|compact|full and --report machine|human; it defaults to a compact machine report. If no fit state is recorded, it reports that there is nothing to undo.

items.title: Output and exit status
items.text: For fit, calc and undo, the selected report is stdout, while warnings and errors are stderr. A failed run exits nonzero. A clean cancellation in the Python package's command lI uses status 130. Report freshness checking uses status 1 when a listed saved report is not current.

items.title: Save and check reports
items.text:
The report command uses the project's structures, experiments, fit results and saved report settings. It presents the same document as Python and the application's Report page.

The shared Report chapter explains the scientific model; the steps below describe this interface.

items.title: Save the selected formats
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report path/to/project

This writes the formats selected by the project into its reports/ folder, for the available writers. HTML and CIF reports are written. The application writes PDF; the command leaves an existing PDF and its record as they are.

Saving a project does not automatically save its report. A report can become out of date after changes to the model or report contents.

items.title: Write an HTML file elsewhere
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report path/to/project --output report.html --offline

--output PATH writes one HTML report without changing the project's saved-report list. --offline embeds chart libraries; --online makes the HTML load them from the web. Both are overrides for this run.

items.title: Choose the contents
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report path/to/project --x-axis d_spacing --exclude data
python -m edi report path/to/project --exclude reflections --exclude correlations
python -m edi report path/to/project --include-all

Optional group keys are charts, correlations, reflections, data and evolution. Repeat --exclude for several groups, or use --include-all. These two choices are mutually exclusive.

items.title: Correlations and colours
items.text:
Option Meaning --x-axis native or d_spacing Use the experiment's native axis or d-spacing. --correlation-threshold X Show parameters whose strongest correlation reaches X, from 0 to 1. --correlation-experiment NAME Choose the experiment for the correlation chart in a multi-experiment fit. --colour-scheme NAME Use earth (the default), classic, soft, natural or colourBlindSafe.

These switches affect the generated report for that run; they do not replace the project's saved preferences.

items.title: Check saved reports
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report path/to/project --check

The command lists each saved report as current, out of date or missing, writing nothing. It exits with status 1 when a listed report is not current. It checks the saved list; it does not require that a project has already saved a report.

items.title: Install the Command line
items.text: Choose the standalone executable to run without Python, or the Python Python package to use python -m edi. Both fit projects from the terminal.

items.title: Standalone Command line
items.text: Run edi without installing Python or setting up a Python environment.

items.title: Download
items.text:
Latest version 2026.11.8 (11 Nov 2026)

macOSmacOS 15+ · Apple Silicon WindowsWindows 11 · x86-64 LinuxUbuntu 24.04+ · x86-64

Extract the ZIP and run ./edi from that folder, or .\edi.exe in Windows PowerShell. Add the folder to your PATH to use edi from other directories.

The standalone executable fits projects with edi fit and prints a final report. Use the Python package route for live progress or for calculation, export, undo, collections, and reports.

items.title: Run a project
items.text:
Open a terminal and check the command:

Standalone executablePython package 
edi --help

python -m edi --help

Pass the saved project and choose where to write the result:

Standalone executablePython package 
edi fit path/to/project --output fitted-project

python -m edi fit path/to/project --output fitted-project

Use Run a fit for the options, or Run an example to try a complete case.

items.title: Structures in a saved project
items.text: Commands calculate from the structures stored in your project and linked by its experiments. They retain the same unit cell, symmetry, atom sites and parameter choices as the application and Python.

items.title: Prepare the structural model
items.text:
Use the application structure controls or Python structure objects to prepare and inspect the structure, then save the complete project.

The command-line interface does not provide a separate structure editor. Its fit and calc commands load the model from the project rather than taking cell and atom-site definitions as command options.

items.title: Check a calculation
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no calc; use the Python package.

python -m edi calc path/to/project --dry

This evaluates the saved model without writing changes. Inspect the output and any errors before starting a fit. See calculate a pattern for output options.

For the common scientific model, read Structure. Continue with Experiments.

items.title: Analysis workflow
items.text:
Follow these stages from a terminal. Commands run on saved projects, so most of the setup lives in the project files.

  1. Project
  2. Structure
  3. Experiment
  4. Analysis
  5. Report
Stage In Command line Project Prepare the input files and find the output files Structure Use the structures prepared in a project Experiment Use the experiments prepared in a project Analysis Calculate a pattern, fit a project and run batches Report Generate a report and check it

The shared analysis workflow explains the science behind each stage.

items.title: Fit with your own AI assistant
items.text: ChatGPT or Claude, in their desktop apps or command-line tools, can write an EasyDiffraction project that edi fit fits. This page gives a prompt for the La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ example of the La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ on HRPT tutorial. The prompt links the documentation and the Command line tutorials, so the assistant can read how EasyDiffraction is used, and it names the fit stages, so the project is fitted in the same order as the tutorial.

items.title: Get the two files
items.text:
Download the structure and the measured pattern from EasyDiffraction's collection into one folder:

  • tutorial-lbco.cif: the cubic perovskite, La and Ba sharing the corner site.
  • tutorial-hrpt.xye: the HRPT pattern, 2θ in degrees, the counts and their standard uncertainties.

items.title: Ask for the project
items.text:
Start the assistant in that folder, or attach the two files to the chat, and give it this prompt:

Fit the crystal structure of La0.5Ba0.5CoO3 to neutron powder diffraction data with
EasyDiffraction (edi).

Documentation: https://easydiffraction.org/ (a short index for assistants:
https://easydiffraction.org/llms.txt).
Worked examples: https://easydiffraction.org/cli/tutorials/ (choose the one closest to this task).

The two input files are in this folder:
- tutorial-lbco.cif: the structure, space group P m -3 m, La and Ba sharing one site.
- tutorial-hrpt.xye: the measured pattern, constant-wavelength neutrons on HRPT at PSI, wavelength
  1.494 Å; columns 2θ (degrees), counts and their standard uncertainties.

Create an EasyDiffraction project, ready for edi fit, that loads both files and fits the structure
in stages.
Each stage frees one more group of parameters and keeps the ones freed before it free:
1. the scale, the 2θ zero and the cell length a;
2. the background points;
3. the peak widths U, V, W and Y;
4. the isotropic displacements (B iso) of La, Ba, Co and O.
After stage 4, show the correlations. La's and Ba's B iso should move together almost exactly.
Constrain Ba's B iso to equal La's, and fit again.

After every fit, show the fitted parameters. At the end, give the reduced χ², Rwp and each fitted
value with its standard uncertainty.

The project it returns should fit with edi fit, from the standalone executable or the Python Python package. Compare its final values with the La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ on HRPT tutorial's: an assistant can pick other starting values or miss a step, and the tutorial shows what each stage should give.

The same prompt, asking for a Jupyter notebook, is on the Python Python tutorials. The application has an AI assistant built in.

items.title: Co₂SiO₄ on D20
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Get the project
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi download-data pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20

python -m edi download-data pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

In experiments/d20.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_instrument.calib_twotheta_offset 0
_peak.broad_gauss_u 0.2
_peak.broad_gauss_v -0.5
_peak.broad_gauss_w 0.4
_peak.broad_lorentz_y 0.01
1 8 340
2 9 340

The same for every other row (13 more).

In structures/cosio.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_cell.length_a 10.3
_cell.length_b 6
_cell.length_c 4.8
Co1 Co 0 0 0 a 4 1 0.5 Biso
Co2 Co 0.28 0.25 0.98 c 4 1 0.5 Biso

The same for every other row (4 more).

items.title: Scale, 2θ zero and cell
items.text:
The scale sets the overall height of the pattern, and the zero shift and the three cell lengths put the peaks where they are measured.

In experiments/d20.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_instrument.calib_twotheta_offset 0()
cosio 1() 1.0

In structures/cosio.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_cell.length_a 10.3()
_cell.length_b 6()

items.title: Constrain the two Co sites
items.text:
The correlations show no strong pair for the two Co sites, yet the fit gives them very different displacements, Co1's even negative, which no atom can have: both are Co and scatter alike, so the pattern cannot tell their thermal motions apart. Give each an alias and constrain Co2's to follow Co1's, starting again from 0.5 Å², then fit again; the shared displacement is positive and its s.u. smaller than either had alone.

In analysis/analysis.edi, add these rows to its alias and constraint loops:

biso_Co1 cosio.atom_site.Co1.adp_iso
biso_Co2 cosio.atom_site.Co2.adp_iso

The same for every other row (1 more).

In structures/cosio.edi, set the values the stage starts again from:

Co1 Co 0 0 0 a 4 1 0.50() Biso

Si Si 0.0933() 0.25 0.4278() c 4 1 0.466 Biso

Co1 0() 1() 0() Mx,My,Mz
Co2 0 1() 0 0,My,0

items.title: Report
items.text:
Write the HTML report of the fitted project and open it in a browser.

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

items.title: Sequential magnetic fit: Co₂SiO₄, D20 scan from 2.3 K
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Get the project
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi download-data pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20_scan-213f

python -m edi download-data pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20_scan-213f

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

In experiments/d20.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_instrument.calib_twotheta_offset 0.29433
_peak.broad_gauss_u 0.273527
_peak.broad_gauss_v -0.589718
_peak.broad_gauss_w 0.413007
1 6 603.5
2 6.5 585

The same for every other row (15 more).

In structures/cosio.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_cell.length_a 10.3081
_cell.length_b 6.00219
_cell.length_c 4.78739
Co1 Co 0 0 0 a 4 1 0.269 Biso
Co2 Co 0.2809 0.25 0.9836 c 4 1 0.269 Biso

The same for every other row (6 more).

items.title: Scale, 2θ zero and cell
items.text:
Switch the fitting mode to a single fit, so the stages fit the template alone.

In analysis/analysis.edi, set:

_fitting_mode.type single

In experiments/d20.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_instrument.calib_twotheta_offset 0.29433()
cosio 1.81723() 1.0

In structures/cosio.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_cell.length_a 10.3081()
_cell.length_b 6.00219()
_cell.length_c 4.78739()

items.title: Rietveld fit: herbertsmithite, HRPT
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.text:

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

In experiments/hrpt.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_peak.broad_gauss_u 0.1
_peak.broad_gauss_v -0.2

_peak.asym_beba_a0 0

_peak.asym_beba_b1 0
1 4 460
2 20 460

_cell.length_a 6.85
_cell.length_c 14.1

Cu Cu 0.5 0 0 e 9 1 0.5 Biso

items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage. The Python tutorial builds this project by hand; here the command line starts from its starting project instead, since building a project by hand on the command line is planned for a later release.

items.title: Constrain La and Ba
items.text:
The correlations show the displacements of La and Ba moving together almost exactly, with opposite signs: they share one site and scatter neutrons similarly, so the pattern cannot tell them apart, and their s.u. are large. Give each an alias and constrain Ba's to follow La's, then fit again. Ba's displacement is no longer fitted on its own.

In analysis/analysis.edi, add these rows to its alias and constraint loops:

biso_La lbco.atom_site.La.adp_iso
biso_Ba lbco.atom_site.Ba.adp_iso

items.title: Rietveld fit: Y₂O₃, SPODI
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.text:

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

_peak.broad_gauss_u 0.04
_peak.broad_gauss_v -0.07
_peak.broad_gauss_w 0.1
1 12.5856 6400
2 19.4181 6400

_cell.length_a 10.61
Y1 Y -0.03 0 0.25 d 24 1 0.49982 beta
O1 O 0.39 0.15 0.38 e 48 1 0.49982 beta

items.title: Scale, 2θ zero and cell
items.text:
Set the background to its automatic estimate in the experiment file: each fit places its points first, by the arPLS method, a smooth curve under the pattern that ignores the peaks. The scale, the zero shift and the cell length put the peaks in place and at the right height.

In experiments/spodi.edi, set:

_background_estimate.mode auto
_background_estimate.n_points 21

In experiments/spodi.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_instrument.calib_twotheta_offset 0()
y2o3 0.1() 1.0

In structures/y2o3.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_cell.length_a 10.61()

items.title: Two-phase fit: YAlO₃ and Al₂O₃, SPODI
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Rietveld fit: CeCoAl₃, POLARIS
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Get the project
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi download-data pd-neut-tof_cecoal-polaris

python -m edi download-data pd-neut-tof_cecoal-polaris

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

In experiments/polaris.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_offset 0
_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_quadratic -1.92194
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_1 40
_peak.broad_lorentz_gamma_1 5
_absorption.abscor1 0
1 0 25000
2 1 0

The same for every other row (11 more).

In structures/cecoal.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_cell.length_a 7.65
_cell.length_b 4.05
_cell.length_c 6.91
Ce Ce 0.25 0 0.38 e 2 1 0.5 Biso
Co Co 0.25 0 0.81 e 2 1 0.5 Biso

The same for every other row (3 more).

items.title: Scale, time-of-flight calibration and cell

_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_offset 0()
_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_quadratic -1.92194()
cecoal 20000() 1.0

_cell.length_a 7.65()
_cell.length_b 4.05()
_cell.length_c 6.91()

items.title: Report
items.text:
Write the HTML report of the fitted project and open it in a browser.

Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report pd-neut-tof_cecoal-polaris --output pd-neut-tof_cecoal-polaris.html

items.title: Calibration fit: CeO₂, PEARL
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Get the project
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi download-data pd-neut-tof_ceo2-pearl

python -m edi download-data pd-neut-tof_ceo2-pearl

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

In experiments/pearl.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_offset 0
_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_linear 4680
_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_quadratic 1.7621
_peak.rise_alpha_1 0.3
_peak.decay_beta_0 0.03
_peak.decay_beta_1 0.03
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_1 80
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_2 4
_peak.broad_lorentz_gamma_1 5
_absorption.abscor1 0
1 0 2200
2 1 0

The same for every other row (5 more).

In structures/ceo2.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

Ce Ce 0 0 0 a 4 1 0.5 Biso
O O 0.25 0.25 0.25 c 8 1 0.5 Biso

items.title: Joint fit: ferrite and austenite, BEER
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Get the project
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi download-data pd-neut-tof_ferrite-austenite-beer

python -m edi download-data pd-neut-tof_ferrite-austenite-beer

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

In experiments/expt_n2.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_offset 0
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_0 900
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_1 1000
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_2 300
_peak.broad_lorentz_gamma_0 5
1 40111.8789 0.19
2 41193.5664 0.19

The same for every other row (28 more).

In experiments/expt_s2.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_offset 0
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_0 900
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_1 1000
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_2 300
_peak.broad_lorentz_gamma_0 5
1 40111.8789 0.18
2 41193.5664 0.18

The same for every other row (30 more).

In structures/ferrite.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

Fe Fe 0 0 0 a 2 1 0.5 Biso

items.title: Scales and time-of-flight calibration
items.text:
Both phases' scales and each bank's DIFC offset put the peaks in place and at the right height.

In experiments/expt_n2.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_offset 0()

In experiments/expt_s2.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_offset 0()
ferrite 400() 0.49780285149965137()
austenite 100() 0.5021971485003485()

items.title: Report

Write the HTML report of the fitted project and open it in a browser.

Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report pd-neut-tof_ferrite-austenite-beer --output pd-neut-tof_ferrite-austenite-beer.html

items.title: Two-phase fit: La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ and Si, McStas
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Get the project
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi download-data pd-neut-tof_lbco-si-mcstas

python -m edi download-data pd-neut-tof_lbco-si-mcstas

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

In experiments/mcstas.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_peak.rise_alpha_1 0.01
_peak.decay_beta_0 0.006
_peak.decay_beta_1 0.004
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_0 50000
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_1 -50000
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_2 20000
1 45000 0.23
2 50000 0.23

The same for every other row (13 more).

In structures/lbco.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_cell.length_a 3.8909
Co Co 0.5 0.5 0.5 b 1 1 0.5 Biso
O O 0 0.5 0.5 c 3 1 0.5 Biso

In structures/si.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_cell.length_a 5.43

items.title: Scales and cells
items.text:
Both phases' scales and cells put the peaks in place and at the right height; the DIFC stays fixed, as in diffraction-lib's tutorial.

In experiments/mcstas.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

lbco 4() 0.8892011305507715()
si 0.2() 0.11079886944922841()

In structures/lbco.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_cell.length_a 3.8909()

In structures/si.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_cell.length_a 5.43()

items.title: Joint fit: Na₂Ca₃Al₂F₁₄, WISH
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Report
items.text:
Write the HTML report of the fitted project and open it in a browser.

Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report pd-neut-tof_ncaf-wish --output pd-neut-tof_ncaf-wish.html

items.title: Rietveld fit: Si, SEPD
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Get the project
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi download-data pd-neut-tof_si-sepd

python -m edi download-data pd-neut-tof_si-sepd

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

In experiments/sepd.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_offset 0
_peak.decay_beta_0 0.04
_peak.decay_beta_1 0.01
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_0 3
_peak.broad_gauss_sigma_1 30
_peak.broad_lorentz_gamma_1 3
1 2000 120
2 9035 120

The same for every other row (13 more).

In structures/si.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_cell.length_a 5.431
Si Si 0.125 0.125 0.125 a 8 1 0.5 Biso

items.title: Cell, scale and time-of-flight calibration
items.text:
Set the background to its automatic estimate in the experiment file: each fit places its points first, by the arPLS method, a smooth curve under the pattern that ignores the peaks.

In experiments/sepd.edi, set:

_background_estimate.mode auto
_background_estimate.n_points 14

In experiments/sepd.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_instrument.calib_d_to_tof_offset 0()
si 600() 1.0

In structures/si.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_cell.length_a 5.431()

items.title: Your own measured data
items.text: The command line fits the files of a project. To start from a measured-data file on your own disk, create the experiment in the Python package with add_from_data_path, or in the app with Load ▾ Measured data From file…, and save the project; creating one from a data file on the command line comes in a later version.

items.title: Report
items.text:
Write the HTML report of the fitted project and open it in a browser.

Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report pd-neut-tof_si-sepd --output pd-neut-tof_si-sepd.html

items.title: Joint fit: PbSO₄, neutron and X-ray
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Rietveld fit: high-entropy perovskite, P02.1
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Sequential fit: LATP, BM01
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Rietveld fit: PbSO₄, laboratory X-ray
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Get the project
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi download-data pd-xray-cwl_pbso4-lab

python -m edi download-data pd-xray-cwl_pbso4-lab

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

In experiments/lab.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_instrument.calib_twotheta_offset 0
_peak.broad_gauss_u 0.02
_peak.broad_gauss_v -0.02
_peak.broad_gauss_w 0.008
_peak.mixing_eta_0 0.5
_peak.asym_beba_a0 0
_peak.asym_beba_b0 0
1 0 140
2 1 0

The same for every other row (5 more).

In structures/pbso4.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

_cell.length_a 8.47
_cell.length_b 5.39
_cell.length_c 6.95
Pb Pb 0.19 0.25 0.17 c 4 1 0.5 Biso
S S 0.07 0.25 0.68 c 4 1 0.5 Biso

The same for every other row (3 more).

items.title: Scale and 2θ zero
items.text:
The 2θ zero first: freed together with the cell from the start, the two pull against each other and the fit cannot take a step.

In experiments/lab.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

_instrument.calib_twotheta_offset 0()
pbso4 0.001() 1.0

items.title: Single-crystal fit: Co₂SiO₄ at three temperatures, HEiDi
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: 2.5 K: the magnetic moments
items.text:

Co1 0() 0() 0() Mx,My,Mz

items.title: Report
items.text:
Write the HTML report of the fitted project and open it in a browser.

Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi --output sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi.html

items.title: Single-crystal fit: Pr₂NiO₄, 5C2
items.text: The same staged fit as the Python tutorial, on the command line. The command line fits whatever the project marks free with () after a value, so each stage marks its parameters in the project's files with a text editor and runs edi fit, which writes the fitted values back into the project for the next stage.

items.title: Get the project
items.text:
Standalone executablePython package 
edi download-data sc-neut-cwl_pr2nio4-5c2

python -m edi download-data sc-neut-cwl_pr2nio4-5c2

items.title: Start with nothing free
items.text:
The project marks what its finished fit frees. Remove every (), so the stages below free one group at a time.

In experiments/llb_5c2.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

pr2nio4 4

In structures/pr2nio4.edi, remove the () from every value; they now read:

Pr Pr 0 0 0.362 i 8 1 0 Bani
O2 O 0 0 0.176 i 8 0.722965 0 Bani

The same for every other row (6 more).

items.title: Scale
items.text:
The scale brings the calculated intensities to the measured ones.

In experiments/llb_5c2.edi, add () after the values the stage frees:

pr2nio4 4()
