items.title: Report
items.text:
Write the HTML report of the fitted project and open it in a browser.

Standalone executablePython package

The standalone executable has no report; use the Python package.

python -m edi report sc-neut-tof_taurine-senju --output sc-neut-tof_taurine-senju.html

items.title: Start here
items.text: This reference explains the models and numerical conventions used to calculate and fit EasyDiffraction projects. The equations apply across the application, Python and the command line; the feature matrix distinguishes what each interface can do.

items.title: Find a physical model
items.text: Physical models lists each model with the questions it answers, grouped from the diffraction itself to the fit.

items.title: Look up a type or parameter
items.text:
• The model catalogue lists the supported model types and what each one does.
  • Parameter explanations link each scientific parameter to its equation, units and model.
  • Conventions fix the notation used throughout this reference.

items.title: Ask an AI assistant about the physics
items.text:
The application's built-in assistant and your own assistant can both read this reference. When you ask a question, name the model and link the parameter or equation; a good answer states the experiment type and the units before it applies an equation.

Your own assistant can start from the assistant index and the machine-readable catalogue, which list every model and parameter page.

items.title: Background models and estimation
items.text: A background contributes an additive baseline to a powder calculation. It is separate from excluded observations, peak-profile tails and the phase scale.

items.title: Line-segment model
items.text:
For anchors \((x_k,b_k)\) and \((x_{k+1},b_{k+1})\),

\[b(x)=b_k+(b_{k+1}-b_k)\frac{x-x_k}{x_{k+1}-x_k}.\]

Outside the anchor range the endpoint intensity is retained. Anchor positions are fixed nodes; the selected intensities can be fit parameters. This is not a linearly extrapolated edge.

items.title: Polynomial model
items.text:
\[b(x)=\sum_m c_m u^m,\qquad u=x/x_0-1.\]

origin is the nonzero normalisation coordinate \(x_0\) in the pattern's axis units. It is not an intensity intercept. The currently admitted polynomial term orders are 0 through 5.

items.title: Chebyshev model
items.text:
\[b(x)=\sum_m c_mT_m(u),\qquad u=\frac{2x-x_{\min}-x_{\max}}{x_{\max}-x_{\min}},\] \[T_0=1,\quad T_1=u,\quad T_{m+1}=2uT_m-T_{m-1}.\]

x_min and x_max define the normalisation domain. The admitted Chebyshev term orders are 0 through 23. These are true Chebyshev coefficients, not powers of the unnormalised angle or time coordinate. Preserve the origin/domain when moving coefficients between projects.

items.title: Automatic estimation
items.text: The estimator proposes a baseline and then editable anchors or series coefficients. The method is distinct from the final fitted background type. Supported method selectors are auto, arpls, snip and fabc; auto resolves to arpls.

items.title: arPLS
items.text:
An iterated penalised smoothing solve uses

\[(W+\lambda D_2^{\mathsf T}D_2)\mathbf z=W\mathbf y,\] \[w_i=\left[1+\exp\left(\frac{2}{s}[r_i-(2s-m)]\right)\right]^{-1},\qquad\mathbf r=\mathbf y-\mathbf z.\]

\(m,s\) describe the negative residual subset; the reweighting suppresses peak contributions. Smoothness controls the penalty rather than a crystallographic parameter.

items.title: SNIP
items.text:
Peak clipping in log-log-square transformed intensity uses

\[v_i=\log[\log(\sqrt{y_i+1}+1)+1],\qquad v_i\leftarrow\min(v_i,(v_{i-w}+v_{i+w})/2).\]

The window and traversal settings determine the sequence of updates; the transform is inverted afterwards. This is an estimation algorithm, not an extra Bragg contribution.

items.title: FABC and anchor reduction
items.text:
FABC classifies baseline versus peak regions using a wavelet/noise criterion, then smooths through the baseline points. Anchor reduction converts the dense baseline to a smaller line-segment model using a noise-scaled vertical tolerance. in_peaks controls whether proposed anchors are moved out of or dropped from peak windows; use_model determines whether calculated peaks are subtracted before estimation.

Inspect the estimate. A missing phase or unsuitable calculated pattern can affect a model-assisted baseline proposal. Fitting the proposed background is a separate step.

items.title: Excluded observations
items.text: An excluded powder interval removes observations from the fitting objective and agreement-factor sums. It does not add a background component or change the definition of the calculated pattern. Retain excluded ranges with the experiment and justify them physically; masking a mismatch does not improve its model. Single-crystal reflection exclusion is a separate planned capability.

items.title: References
items.text:
1. Baek, S.-J., Park, A., Ahn, Y.-J. & Choo, J. (2015). Baseline correction using asymmetrically reweighted penalized least squares smoothing. Analyst, 140, 250–257. DOI. arPLS baseline estimation.
  2. Ryan, C. G., Clayton, E., Griffin, W. L., Sie, S. H. & Cousens, D. R. (1988). SNIP, a statistics-sensitive background treatment for the quantitative analysis of PIXE spectra in geoscience applications. Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research B, 34, 396–402. DOI. SNIP peak clipping.
  3. Cobas, J. C., Bernstein, M. A., Martín-Pastor, M. & García Tahoces, P. (2006). A new general-purpose fully automatic baseline-correction procedure for 1D and 2D NMR data. Journal of Magnetic Resonance, 183, 145–151. DOI. FABC baseline classification.

items.title: Calibration and peak positions
items.text: Calibration determines where a reflection appears on the experimental axis. It can therefore correlate strongly with fitted cell dimensions.

items.title: Constant-wavelength position
items.text:
\[2\theta_h=\frac{360}{\pi}\arcsin\left(\frac{\lambda}{2d_h}\right),\qquad x_{\rm corrected}=x_{\rm observed}-z.\]

The angle returned by the position equation is in degrees; \(z\) is calib_twotheta_offset, also in degrees \(2\theta\). The corrected coordinate must remain in the admitted open angular range for calculated points. Wavelength and cell changes both affect reflection positions; check their physical meaning before fitting both freely.

items.title: Displacement and transparency shifts
items.text:
The implemented CW reflection-centre shift is

\[\Delta(2\theta_h)=D\cos(2\theta_h)+T\sin(2\theta_h),\]

where \(D\) is calib_sample_displacement and \(T\) is calib_sample_transparency, in degrees \(2\theta\). It is applied to each reflection centre. The zero offset remains on the corrected observed axis. In particular, the displacement term here uses \(\cos2\theta\), not an assumed Bragg–Brentano \(\cos\theta\) formula.

items.title: Time-of-flight position
items.text:
\[t_h=z+D_1d_h+D_2d_h^2.\]

\(z\) is in µs, \(D_1\) in µs/Å and \(D_2\) in µs/Å². The physical positive-spacing branch of the inverse quadratic is used; a negative quadratic coefficient does not by itself justify switching to the other mathematical root.

The reciprocal coefficient calib_d_to_tof_reciprocal (\(D_{-1}/d\)) is read and saved, but not used in the calculation.

items.title: Fixed bank angle
items.text:
A TOF bank uses its declared scattering angle to determine \(\theta_{\rm bank}\) and \(\lambda_h=2d_h\sin\theta_{\rm bank}\). Keep the bank geometry with calibration and absorption settings when moving or comparing a project.

See instrument parameters, Bragg's law and TOF profiles.

items.title: Conventions
items.text: A physical model is reproducible only when its quantities, units and conventions are identified. Keep them with the structure, experiment and analysis settings.

items.title: Axes and units
items.text:
Quantity Convention to check Constant-wavelength powder axis The measured scattering angle is 2θ, in degrees for the powder text input Time-of-flight powder axis Time of flight in microseconds for the powder text input Unit cell Length and angle units, space-group setting and coordinate system Atom positions Fractional coordinates in the selected cell and setting Peak width Whether the quantity is a full width, half width, standard deviation or model-specific coefficient Observation uncertainty A standard uncertainty, rather than a variance or an intensity weight

Use data formats and the relevant import instructions to prepare observations. Changing a filename extension does not convert an axis or unit.

items.title: Atomic displacement parameters
items.text:
Isotropic displacement can be expressed with Uiso or Biso, related by Biso = 8π² Uiso. Both have dimensions of length squared, but their numerical values differ.

Anisotropic displacement uses components in a specified basis. Keep the source convention and coordinate system when importing, exporting or comparing values. See the IUCr displacement-parameter nomenclature and coreCIF B-parameter definition.

items.title: Parameter and file names
items.text: Python access paths, Edi project keys and scientific CIF names have different roles. Use the Python reference for code and data formats for persistence; identify the actual scientific quantity before comparing a similarly named value.

items.title: Comparing calculations
items.text:
Match the structure setting, radiation and scattering sources, instrument calibration, profile definition, background, exclusions, observations and free parameters. Record the software version and minimizer conditions as well.

A comparison is meaningful only for the models and conditions it covers. Retain the complete project and its report with the result.

items.title: Cell metric and spacing
items.text:
Cell lengths \(a,b,c\) and angles \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) define the direct metric

\[ G=\begin{pmatrix}a^2&ab\cos\gamma&ac\cos\beta\\ab\cos\gamma&b^2&bc\cos\alpha\\ac\cos\beta&bc\cos\alpha&c^2\end{pmatrix},\qquad V=\sqrt{\det G},\qquad G^*=G^{-1}. \]

For reflection indices \(\mathbf h=(h,k,l)^{\mathsf T}\),

\[d_{hkl}^{-2}=\mathbf h^{\mathsf T}G^*\mathbf h.\]

Lengths are in Å, angles are entered in degrees, and the trigonometric functions use the corresponding angles. The reciprocal metric above excludes a \(2\pi\) factor. The scattering-vector magnitude is \(Q=2\pi/d\).

items.title: Bragg condition
items.text:
\[2d\sin\theta=n\lambda,\qquad s=\sin\theta/\lambda=1/(2d).\]

For an indexed reflection the order can be incorporated in its Miller indices. The measured powder angle is \(2\theta\), not \(\theta\). A CW reflection is reachable only when \(\lambda/(2d)<1\) in the implemented open-angle domain. See calibration for how this becomes an experimental coordinate.

items.title: Symmetry and atom positions
items.text:
Space-group operations map fractional positions as \(\mathbf r'=R\mathbf r+\mathbf t\) modulo lattice translations. The selected setting fixes the coordinate convention. Symmetry may relate cell parameters or fix atom coordinates; such values are not additional independent fitting directions.

The asymmetric unit and its symmetry-generated images define the unit cell. Wyckoff positions describe site symmetry and multiplicity. Do not count identical special-position images twice or confuse a site's multiplicity with the multiplicity of a reflection.

items.title: Reflection multiplicity and absences
items.text:
Equivalent reciprocal-lattice vectors contribute a reflection multiplicity to a powder intensity. Centering, glide and screw translations can cause systematic absences through phase cancellation in the structure factor. A reflection's symmetry equivalence is a property of its space-group setting and radiation model; a count of atom sites is not its multiplicity.

For practical input, see Structure. Scattering connects the positions to intensities.

items.title: References
items.text: 1. International Union of Crystallography. Bragg's law.

items.title: Nuclear structure factor
items.text:
\[F_N(\mathbf h)=\sum_j o_j b_j T_j(\mathbf h)\exp[2\pi i\,\mathbf h\cdot\mathbf r_j].\]

The sum is over the symmetry-generated cell: \(o_j\) is occupancy, \(b_j\) coherent neutron scattering length, \(T_j\) the displacement factor, and \(\mathbf r_j\) the fractional position. The measured nuclear intensity uses \(|F_N|^2\) with the applicable scale and measurement factors. The sign of the exponential is a phase convention; it must be kept consistent with any complex scattering contribution.

Neutron scattering lengths depend on species/isotope, not on the X-ray atomic form-factor equation. The supported source selectors are rauch2003ext and sears1992; preserve the selected source or explicitly supplied scattering lengths when reproducing a calculation. Model admission rules prevent conflicting source declarations.

items.title: X-ray form factors and dispersion
items.text:
For the scalar X-ray model, replace \(b_j\) by

\[f_j(s,\lambda)=f_{0,j}(s)+f'_j(\lambda)+i f''_j(\lambda),\qquad s=\sin\theta/\lambda.\]

Tabulated Gaussian parameterisations have the form

\[f_0(s)=c+\sum_{n=1}^{M}a_n\exp(-b_n s^2).\]

wk1995 and it1992 select the supported form-factor tables, with their own coefficient sets. Dispersion selectors are cromer-liberman, sasaki1989, it1992 and none. none omits the anomalous-dispersion term; it does not replace the atom's normal form factor by zero.

These selectors identify data sources, not alternative calculation engines. Keep the source and wavelength with the project, especially near an absorption edge. See model coverage.

items.title: Occupancy and scale
items.text: Occupancy weights an atom's contribution to the structure factor. A phase scale weights the phase's intensity contribution to an experiment. Changing one is not generally equivalent to changing the other, and they can be strongly correlated with displacement and composition choices.

items.title: Multiple phases and mass fractions
items.text:
An experiment sums the contributions of its enabled structure links. In the conventional scale-to-weight relation,

\[w_p=\frac{s_p Z_p M_p V_p}{\sum_q s_q Z_q M_q V_q}.\]

Here \(Z_pM_p\) is the cell formula mass and \(V_p\) its volume; a cell-mass representation uses the same product without separately spelling \(Z\) and formula mass. Interpret reported fractions with the project's scale convention, composition and links. A disconnected structure contributes no intensity.

items.title: Magnetic diffraction
items.text: Commensurate magnetic structures are available for unpolarised neutron powder data. Magnetic scattering involves vector contributions beyond the scalar nuclear and X-ray models above; see Magnetic structures.

items.title: Polarised diffraction
items.text: Planned. Polarised diffraction is planned. Polarization changes the scattering cross-section; the scalar model above does not provide this capability.

items.title: Total scattering and PDF
items.text:
Planned. Total scattering and pair distribution function (PDF) analysis are planned. PDF uses a total-scattering transform rather than the Bragg-profile model.

See Scattering models for the status of these and the implemented models.

items.title: References
items.text: 1. International Union of Crystallography. Structure factor.

items.title: Atomic displacement parameters
items.text: Displacement parameters describe the attenuation of coherent scattering by the distribution of positions around each site's average position. Their conventions and coordinate basis matter.

items.title: Isotropic forms
items.text:
\[T_{\rm iso}(s)=\exp(-B_{\rm iso}s^2)=\exp(-8\pi^2U_{\rm iso}s^2),\qquad B_{\rm iso}=8\pi^2U_{\rm iso}.\]

Both Biso and Uiso have units Å². An equal numerical value in the two forms does not represent equal displacement. adp_type chooses Biso or Uiso; adp_iso carries the corresponding value.

items.title: Anisotropic forms
items.text:
With fractional reflection indices and reciprocal-cell lengths,

\[T_{\rm aniso}=\exp\left[-2\pi^2\sum_{i,j}U_{ij}h_i h_j a_i^*a_j^*\right] =\exp\left[-\tfrac14\sum_{i,j}B_{ij}h_i h_j a_i^*a_j^*\right].\]

The beta convention absorbs the reciprocal-length and \(2\pi^2\) factors:

\[T_{\rm aniso}=\exp[-\mathbf h^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta\mathbf h].\]

Bani, Uani and beta are distinct supported representations. The six independent symmetric components include cross terms: a full \(\sum_{i,j}\) counts \(ij\) and \(ji\), so an off-diagonal entry must not be added as if it were already doubled. Space-group symmetry can constrain the components.

items.title: Interpretation
items.text: Check physical plausibility and positive-definiteness where appropriate. A large displacement can compensate for another model error; its fitted uncertainty does not resolve that ambiguity. Link the value to the parameter index and the selected convention before discussing it with the assistant.

items.title: References
items.text:
1. International Union of Crystallography. Atomic displacement parameter nomenclature. Definitions and coordinate conventions.
  2. International Union of Crystallography. coreCIF definition of isotropic B.

items.title: Magnetic structures
items.text:
EasyDiffraction calculates and fits commensurate magnetic structures from unpolarised neutron powder data, at constant wavelength and in time of flight. One structure carries both the nuclear and the magnetic scattering: one set of atoms and one scale, not a separate magnetic phase.

Current coverage

The calculation covers a commensurate structure with propagation vector \(\mathbf k=0\), whose magnetic space group's spatial operations form a setting of the space-group table. Non-zero \(\mathbf k\), grey groups, operators that form no table setting, magCIF import and polarised diffraction are not available yet. A neutron single-crystal experiment linked to a magnetic structure adds the magnetic intensity \(|\mathbf M_\perp|^2\) to each reflection, and its fit can free the moments.

items.title: The magnetic cell
items.text: A magnetic structure is stored in its magnetic cell, as magCIF writes it. The cell, every atom, the operators and the centring vectors all belong to that cell, and reflections are integer \(hkl\) of it. The parent space group and its propagation vectors are recorded with the structure; each vector must be one the magnetic cell can carry.

items.title: Magnetic symmetry
items.text:
Each operator of the magnetic space group is a spatial operation \(\{R|\mathbf t\}\) with a time-reversal sign \(\theta=\pm1\), written as, for example, x,y,z,+1.

Symmetry limits the moment a site can carry. Written in lattice-vector components \(\mu_i=M_i/a_i\), a moment is allowed when every signed operation that fixes the site leaves it unchanged:

\[\theta\,\det(R)\,R\,\boldsymbol\mu=\boldsymbol\mu.\]

The components this leaves dependent or fixed are not fitted independently, as with symmetry-fixed coordinates. The derived form is shown as the site's symmetry form, for example Mx,My,Mz or 0,My,0.

items.title: Moment components
items.text:
A moment is stored and fitted in crystal-axis components, in Bohr magnetons along unit vectors parallel to \(\mathbf a\), \(\mathbf b\) and \(\mathbf c\). It can also be shown in two other forms:

  • Cartesian, in magCIF's frame: \(x\) along \(\mathbf a\), \(z\) along \(\mathbf c^*\), and \(y\) completing a right-handed set.
  • Spherical: the modulus, the polar angle from \(+z\), and the azimuthal angle from \(+x\) around \(+z\).

After a fit, the uncertainties of the derived values come from the fit's covariance, including correlations. Before a fit they are propagated as if the crystal-axis components were uncorrelated. A value the moment does not determine, such as the angles of a zero moment, has no uncertainty.

items.title: Magnetic form factor
items.text:
With \(s=\sin\theta/\lambda\),

\[f(s)=\langle j_0\rangle(s)+C_2\langle j_2\rangle(s)+C_4\langle j_4\rangle(s)+C_6\langle j_6\rangle(s),\]

where each higher \(\langle j_n\rangle\) carries its \(s^2\) factor, using the coefficients of International Tables Vol. C §4.4.5. Each atom type chooses an approximation:

Approximation Terms used j0 \(\langle j_0\rangle\) alone dipole \(\langle j_0\rangle+C_2\langle j_2\rangle\) beyond_dipole All four terms

\(C_2\), \(C_4\) and \(C_6\) are parameters that can be fitted. A coefficient the approximation does not use is ignored, and one whose term the ion's table lacks must stay 0. The model carries no convention for the Landé factor \(g\): \(C_2=2/g-1\) for a moment counted against \(J\), and \(1-2/g\) against \(S\).

items.title: Magnetic structure factor
items.text:
Over the atoms of the magnetic cell, with the same phase sign and displacement factor as the nuclear structure factor,

\[\mathbf M(\mathbf h)=p\sum_j o_j f_j(s)\,T_j(\mathbf h)\,\theta_j\det(R_j)\,(A R_j A^{-1})\,\mathbf m_j\,\exp[2\pi i\,\mathbf h\cdot\mathbf r_j].\]

Here \(p=2.695\) fm per Bohr magneton, \(o_j\) is occupancy, \(\mathbf m_j\) the site's moment, and \(A\) takes lattice components to Cartesian ones. Only the component perpendicular to the scattering vector contributes:

\[\mathbf M_\perp=\mathbf M-(\hat{\mathbf e}\cdot\mathbf M)\,\hat{\mathbf e}.\]

items.title: Intensity
items.text:
For unpolarised neutrons, the nuclear and magnetic parts add without interference:

\[I\propto|F_N|^2+|\mathbf M_\perp|^2.\]

The magnetic intensity uses the same profile, scale and corrections as the nuclear one, so both share every instrument model. With every moment at zero, the pattern equals that of the same structure without magnetic categories. X-ray experiments use the nuclear rule only.

A reflection is generated when either its nuclear or its magnetic sum over the stabiliser of \(\mathbf h\) is non-zero, so purely magnetic reflections are included.

items.title: Nuclear and magnetic parts of a pattern
items.text: Each structure's curve is also available in two parts. The magnetic part is the same profile drawn from \(|\mathbf M_\perp|^2\) alone, and the nuclear part is the net curve less it, so the two add up to the net curve exactly. Each reflection records its nuclear \(|F|^2\), its \(|F_{M\perp}|^2\) and their total.

items.title: Fitting moments
items.text:
Moment components and form-factor coefficients are fitted with analytical derivatives, like other structural parameters. Freeing either on X-ray data is refused, because X-rays do not measure them here.

The magnetic intensity is quadratic in the moment, which makes \(\mathbf M=0\) hard for an ordinary step to reach: near zero, the step grows as \(1/M\) and overshoots. This matters above an ordering temperature. By default, once a fit is nearly finished, each iteration therefore also tries every free moment component at exactly zero together, and keeps that point when \(\chi^2\) is lower. _minimizer.moments_near_zero chooses this behaviour (try_exact_zero) or leaves the moments free to move (keep_free).

See minimization and uncertainty for the fit itself and Magnetic moments for the application's controls.

items.title: Independent parameters and Jacobian
items.text:
For the weighted residual vector \(\mathbf r\) defined in Rietveld method, let \(J_{ij}=\partial r_i/\partial p_j\). The Jacobian columns correspond to independent free parameters; fixed, symmetry-related and constrained dependent values are not extra columns.

The scientific models and their derivatives share their declared parameter conventions. A parameter that is only stored has no nonzero model derivative merely because a numerical value is present in the file.

items.title: Levenberg–Marquardt step
items.text:
A scaled damped least-squares step has the form

\[(J^{\mathsf T}J+\lambda D)\Delta\mathbf p=-J^{\mathsf T}\mathbf r.\]

\(D\) supplies the diagonal scaling/damping convention; \(\lambda\) controls damping. The implemented strategy controls the acceptance and damping search, while the scientific objective remains the weighted residual sum.

Descent selector Meaning ladder Damping-ladder LM search fast_descent Gain-ratio damping within each step multistart_prune Fast descent and the ladder run briefly from the start; the lower continues (the default)

The project records its descent, positive relative objective tolerance and positive iteration budget. A budget stop is not the same as convergence. Some strategies have restrictions when bounds are declared; inspect the reported diagnostic rather than assuming every combination is supported.

items.title: Covariance and standard uncertainties
items.text:
At the final state, the current covariance convention is the scaled inverse curvature

\[C=\chi^2_{\rm red}(J^{\mathsf T}J)^+,\qquad u(p_j)=\sqrt{\max(C_{jj},0)},\qquad \rho_{jk}=C_{jk}/\sqrt{C_{jj}C_{kk}}.\]

The Jacobian here is already weighted. The implementation computes a column-scaled pseudoinverse and transforms back to physical parameter units, using the undamped final curvature. The + denotes that numerical pseudoinverse; it is not an inverse of the damped LM step matrix.

The reduced-χ² scaling is an explicit convention. Do not silently substitute an unscaled covariance from another program. A zero-sensitivity direction or numerical degeneracy requires inspecting the associated diagnostics; a zero reported uncertainty does not make an unmeasured parameter exact.

items.title: Constraints and bounds
items.text:
A constraint relates quantities and reduces independent freedom. Physical admissibility limits, editable optimizer bounds and symmetry restrictions serve different purposes. The application's displayed minimum and maximum are model-admissibility information; they are not a promise of controls for setting optimizer search bounds.

Use Parameters for practical interpretation. The fit's observation set and parameter count also determine the reliability factors.

items.title: Global minimization (planned)
items.text: Least squares improves a fit from its starting values, so a poor start can leave it in a local minimum. A global search, such as simulated annealing or several fits from different starting points, is planned to find a better start before the least-squares fit.

items.text:

items.title: Reliability factors
items.text: Reliability factors summarise agreement under a defined observation model. They supplement the pattern, residual, physical model and parameter uncertainties.

items.title: Included observations and weights
items.text: For powder factors, sums run over included points outside excluded intervals with positive standard uncertainty and available finite calculated intensity. Let \(w_i=1/\sigma_i^2\), \(b_i\) be background, \(N\) the included point count and \(P\) the independent free-parameter count.

items.title: Powder profile factors
items.text:
\[R_p=\frac{\sum_i|y_{o,i}-y_{c,i}|}{\sum_i|y_{o,i}|},\qquad R_{wp}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_iw_i(y_{o,i}-y_{c,i})^2}{\sum_iw_i y_{o,i}^2}},\] \[R_{\exp}=\sqrt{\frac{N-P}{\sum_iw_i y_{o,i}^2}},\qquad \chi^2_{\rm red}=\frac{\sum_iw_i(y_{o,i}-y_{c,i})^2}{N-P}.\]

The engine's factor values are fractions; a displayed percentage is 100 times that fraction. \(R_{wp}/R_{\exp}\) is the square root of reduced χ² under matching sums and degrees of freedom. The name “goodness of fit” is used for both conventions in the literature, so state which is meant.

A fit needs positive degrees of freedom to interpret reduced χ². Nonpositive degrees of freedom or a zero denominator are degenerate cases; the report's numerical guard result is not a statistically meaningful factor.

items.title: Background-subtracted factors
items.text:
The conventional background-subtracted factors retain the same residual numerator but replace the normalising observations by net intensity:

\[cR_p=\frac{\sum_i|y_{o,i}-y_{c,i}|}{\sum_i|y_{o,i}-b_i|},\qquad cR_{wp}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_iw_i(y_{o,i}-y_{c,i})^2}{\sum_iw_i(y_{o,i}-b_i)^2}},\] \[cR_{\exp}=\sqrt{\frac{N-P}{\sum_iw_i(y_{o,i}-b_i)^2}}.\]

Removing background from the denominator can change the apparent factor substantially. Do not compare a conventional profile Rwp directly with a background-subtracted value while calling them the same definition.

items.title: Bragg and F factors
items.text:
Powder phase factors use reflection intensities apportioned from the observed profile according to the calculated contributions:

\[I_{o,h}=\sum_i I_{c,h}(i)\frac{y_{o,i}-b_i}{y_{c,i}-b_i},\qquad R_B=\frac{\sum_h|I_{o,h}-I_{c,h}|}{\sum_h|I_{o,h}|}.\] \[|F_{c,h}|=\sqrt{m_h|F_h|^2},\qquad |F_{o,h}|=|F_{c,h}|\sqrt{\max(I_{o,h},0)/I_{c,h}},\qquad R_F=\frac{\sum_h\big||F_{o,h}|-|F_{c,h}|\big|}{\sum_h|F_{o,h}|}.\]

The reflection partition is model-dependent, particularly where peaks overlap. These phase factors are not independent directly measured integrated intensities for every powder reflection.

items.title: Single-crystal reflection factors
items.text:
The reflection-statistics view also reports amplitude-based and intensity-weighted factors over a declared set \(\mathcal H\):

\[R(F)=\frac{\sum_{h\in\mathcal H}\left|\sqrt{\max(F_{o,h}^2,0)}-\sqrt{\max(F_{c,h}^2,0)}\right|}{\sum_{h\in\mathcal H}\sqrt{\max(F_{o,h}^2,0)}},\] \[wR(F^2)=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{h\in\mathcal H}w_h(F_{o,h}^2-F_{c,h}^2)^2}{\sum_{h\in\mathcal H}w_h(F_{o,h}^2)^2}},\qquad w_h=1/u(F_{o,h}^2)^2.\]

r_factor_all and wr_factor_all use all reflections; _gt uses those passing the experiment's observed-reflection threshold; wr_factor_ref uses those selected for fitting. An absent observed threshold means \(I>2u(I)\). An amplitude threshold \(F>n u(F)\) is implemented as \(F_o^2>(n/2)u(F_o^2)\); an intensity threshold uses \(F_o^2>n u(F_o^2)\). The project's optional fit threshold is separate and uses the intensity rule. A reporting threshold does not itself discard weak data from fitting.

items.title: Single-crystal reflection exclusions
items.text: Planned. Single-crystal reflection exclusions are planned. The reporting and fit-threshold rules above describe the current behaviour. See Background and excluded observations for the status alongside powder exclusions.

items.title: Per-experiment and pooled summaries
items.text:
For a single-crystal reflection list, the same absolute and weighted formulas operate on observed and calculated \(F^2\) values, giving \(R(F^2)\) and \(wR(F^2)\). There is no powder background partition; the background-subtracted denominators equal the un-subtracted ones. Do not label this intensity-based factor as the amplitude-based \(R(F)\).

Per-experiment factors use that experiment's included observations. Pooled factors combine the underlying sums across experiments; they are not an arithmetic average of each experiment's R factor. Keep the objective weighting and factor definition explicit when interpreting joint fits.

items.title: Interpretation
items.text: There is no universal threshold that proves structural correctness. Changing the data range, uncertainty estimates, background, excluded observations or free set changes the statistic. See assessing a fit.

items.title: References
items.text:
1. McCusker, L. B., Von Dreele, R. B., Cox, D. E., Louër, D. & Scardi, P. (1999). Rietveld refinement guidelines. Journal of Applied Crystallography, 32, 36–50.
  2. Toby, B. H. (2006). R factors in Rietveld analysis: How good is good enough? Powder Diffraction, 21, 67–70.

items.title: Rietveld method
items.text: The Rietveld method compares a calculated powder pattern with measured intensities over the included observations. It fits a crystallographic model together with the relevant experiment parameters.

items.title: Calculated powder pattern
items.text:
A useful decomposition is

\[ y_i^{\rm calc}=b(x_i)+\sum_p s_p\sum_{h\in p}m_h\,L_h\,P_h\,A_h\,O_h\,|F_h|^2\,\Omega_p(x_i-x_h). \]

Here \(p\) labels a linked phase, \(s_p\) its scale, \(h\) a reflection, \(m_h\) multiplicity, \(L_h\) the geometry-dependent Lorentz factor, \(P_h\) polarization where applicable, \(A_h\) absorption, \(O_h\) preferred orientation, \(F_h\) the structure factor, \(\Omega\) the selected peak profile and \(b\) the background. This is a model decomposition: factors that do not apply to the selected experiment are unity, and instrument-specific intensity-unit conventions are carried with its scale.

Follow the terms to crystallography, scattering, profiles, absorption, orientation, Lorentz/polarization and background. Single-crystal reflection calculations use the corresponding integrated-intensity model, not a powder-profile sum.

items.title: Least-squares objective
items.text:
\[ r_i(\mathbf p)=\frac{y_i^{\rm calc}(\mathbf p)-y_i^{\rm obs}}{\sigma_i},\qquad S(\mathbf p)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}r_i^2. \]

\(\mathcal I\) is the included observation set and \(\sigma_i>0\) its standard uncertainty. Reversing every residual's sign leaves \(S\) unchanged. The displayed observed-minus-calculated difference curve can therefore have the opposite sign to the solver residual.

Only independent free parameters are optimisation variables. Symmetry, constraints, the selected experiment and model type determine which quantities are independent and affect the observations. See minimization.

items.title: Single and joint fitting
items.text:
A single fit uses one experiment. A joint fit combines the residuals of several experiments, sharing their common structural quantities while retaining experiment-specific terms. If experiment weights \(v_e\) are applied, its residual block is multiplied by \(\sqrt{v_e}\) and its objective contribution by \(v_e\).

Inspect each experiment after a joint fit. Combined agreement can hide a systematic mismatch in one dataset. Reliability factors distinguish per-experiment and pooled summaries.

items.title: Sequential and independent scans
items.text: Both scan modes run a sequence of fits against a template experiment. Their distinction is the starting model, not parallel execution. See the fitting-mode guide.

items.title: Sequential scans
items.text: Each dataset starts from the preceding fitted result. This carries the evolving model forward through the series.

items.title: Independent scans
items.text: Every dataset starts from the same template values, so the starting model does not depend on the preceding fit.

items.title: Intensity extraction
items.text: Proposed. These methods are not available fitting modes in this reference snapshot. See Pattern fitting for current alternatives.

items.title: Le Bail intensity extraction
items.text: Reflection intensities are updated by iterative decomposition of the measured powder pattern, alongside profile fitting.

items.title: Pawley intensity extraction
items.text:
Reflection intensities are adjustable variables in a least-squares fit of the powder pattern.

The distinction is described in the IUCr intensity-extraction overview.

items.title: Interpretation
items.text: Fitting improves agreement under the model and its uncertainties. Convergence does not establish that the phase model, background, calibration or uncertainty estimates are correct. Use the practical fit assessment and retain the starting project.

items.title: References
items.text: 1. McCusker, L. B., Von Dreele, R. B., Cox, D. E., Louër, D. & Scardi, P. (1999). Rietveld refinement guidelines. Journal of Applied Crystallography, 32, 36–50.

items.title: Intensity corrections
items.text:
Factors that change a reflection's intensity between the structure factor and the measurement.

Topic Questions answered Absorption Cylinder Hewat and Lobanov transmission, beam-mode differences and active parameters Extinction Becker–Coppens type I, type II and mixed, and isotropic and anisotropic Larson Preferred orientation March–Dollase texture and random fraction Lorentz and polarization Which intensity factors apply to each geometry and radiation probe?

items.title: Absorption
items.text: Absorption reduces the intensity leaving the sample. The cylinder models below apply a multiplicative transmission \(A\) to each reflection's intensity; they do not move the reflection or define a single-crystal extinction correction.

items.title: Types and active fields
items.text:
Beam mode Saved type Active field Meaning CW none — \(A=1\) CW cylinder-hewat mu_r Hewat cylinder expansion CW cylinder-lobanov mu_r Two-branch Lobanov cylinder fit TOF none — \(A=1\) TOF cylinder abscor1 Wavelength-dependent Hewat cylinder; canonical model token cylinder-hewat

For a cylinder, \(\mu R\) uses the radius, not the diameter. It is dimensionless when \(\mu\) and \(R\) use reciprocal length units consistently.

items.title: Hewat cylinder
items.text:
Let \(u=\mu R\) and \(s=\sin\theta\):

\[A(u,\theta)=\exp[-(1.7133-0.0368s^2)u+(0.0927+0.375s^2)u^2].\]

In CW the angle is each reflection's Bragg angle and \(u\) is the mu_r parameter. The polynomial is a small-to-moderate-absorption approximation. At large \(u\) its quadratic exponent is not a general physical transmission law; use an appropriate model and inspect the resulting transmission rather than treating extrapolation as validated physics.

For TOF at a fixed bank angle,

\[\lambda_h=2d_h\sin\theta_{\rm bank},\qquad u_h=\text{ABSCOR1}\,\lambda_h.\]

The same Hewat expression uses that bank angle and reflection-specific wavelength. ABSCOR1 therefore carries the inverse-wavelength scale needed to produce \(u_h\).

FullProf's second coefficient, ABSCOR2, has no effect on this correction, so edi does not have it. An older project file that sets it loads with a warning that the value is ignored.

items.title: Lobanov cylinder
items.text:
For CW cylinder-lobanov, put \(s=\sin\theta\) and \(u=\mu R\). For \(u\le3\):

\[A=\exp[-t_0u-t_1u^2-t_2u^3-t_3u^4],\qquad t_0=16/(3\pi),\] \[\begin{aligned} t_1={}&(25.99978-0.01911\sqrt{s})e^{-0.024551s^2}+0.109561s-26.04556,\\ t_2={}&-0.02489-0.39499s^2+1.219077s^3-1.31268s^4+0.871081s^5-0.2327s^6,\\ t_3={}&0.003045+0.018167s^2-0.03305s^4. \end{aligned}\]

For \(u>3\):

\[A=0.01\left[\frac{t_1-t_4}{(1+t_2(u-3))^{t_3}}+t_4\right],\] \[\begin{aligned} t_1={}&1.433902+11.07504s^2-8.77629s^4+10.02088s^6-3.36778s^8,\\ t_2={}&(0.013869-0.01249s^2)e^{3.27094s^2}+\frac{0.337894+13.77317s^2}{(1+11.53544s^2)^{1.555039}},\\ t_3={}&\frac{1.933433}{(1+23.12967s^2)^{1.686715}}-0.13576s+1.163198,\\ t_4={}&0.044365-\frac{0.04259}{(1+0.41051s^2)^{148.4202}}. \end{aligned}\]

The high-\(u\) expression is tabulated as a percentage before the \(0.01\) conversion to a transmission fraction. The two empirical branches have a small seam mismatch; do not impose an invented continuity correction when reproducing this model.

items.title: References
items.text:
1. Hewat, A. W. (1979). Acta Crystallographica A, 35, 248. Cylinder absorption approximation.
  2. Lobanov, N. N. & Alte da Veiga, L. (1998). Cylinder-transmission parameterisation, as used by the GSAS-II absorption implementation. The coefficients and branch conventions reproduced above identify the implemented approximation.

items.title: Extinction
items.text: Extinction reduces strong single-crystal reflection intensities relative to the kinematic model. It is distinct from sample absorption. The correction below is a factor \(y\) on intensity \(F^2\), not a factor to apply unchanged to an amplitude.

items.title: Single-crystal intensity
items.text:
The scalar nuclear calculation compares each measured reflection with

\[F_{c,h}^2=s\,y_h\,|F_{N,h}|^2.\]

Here \(s\) is the linked structure's scale and \(y_h\) the selected extinction factor. A CW experiment supplies one wavelength; a TOF reflection list supplies a wavelength per reflection. This is a reflection model, with no powder-profile convolution or background term. Keep the structure factor, scale and reflection-statistics convention consistent with the observed \(F^2\) data.

items.title: Supported types
items.text:
Type Physical/empirical model Active inputs none Identity, \(y=1\) — becker-coppens-type-1 Mosaic-spread-limited secondary extinction Crystal radius, mosaic spread, mosaic distribution becker-coppens-type-2 Domain-size-limited secondary extinction with primary extinction Crystal radius, domain radius becker-coppens-mixed Primary and secondary extinction with both finite terms Crystal radius, domain radius, mosaic spread, mosaic distribution larson-isotropic Empirical isotropic factor coefficient larson-anisotropic Direction-dependent empirical coefficient Six coefficient_ij terms

Becker–Coppens mosaic distributions are gaussian and lorentzian. These are extinction distributions, not the powder peak-profile selector.

items.title: Units and common factor
items.text:
Use \(c=\cos2\theta\), \(q=\sin2\theta\), wavelength \(\lambda\) in Å and cell volume \(V\) in Å³. The extinction formula consumes \(F^2\) in \((10^{-12}\,\mathrm{cm})^2\); a structure-factor value in fm must be converted before inserting it.

domain_radius \(r\) is in µm. crystal_radius \(R_c\) is in mm and sets the spherical path \(\ell=1000R_c\) in µm. It is a descriptor, not a fitted domain radius. mosaic_spread \(g\) is an inverse width in rad⁻¹: larger values describe a narrower mosaic distribution. For the mixed Å/µm convention in the expressions below define \(\tilde g=10^{-4}g\).

Define

\[Y(x;a,b,k)=\left[1+kx+\frac{ax^2}{1+bx}\right]^{-1/2}.\]

Do not insert an arcminute mosaic width or a crystal diameter in place of these quantities.

items.title: Secondary Becker–Coppens factor
items.text:
The effective domain \(D\) is

\[D_G=\frac{r\tilde g}{\sqrt{\tilde g^2\lambda^2+\tfrac98r^2q^2}},\qquad D_L=\frac{r\tilde g}{\tilde g\lambda+rq}.\]

Type I takes the unlimited-domain limit: \(D_G=\tilde g/(\sqrt{9/8}\,q)\) and \(D_L=\tilde g/q\). Type II takes the unlimited-mosaic-spread limit \(D=r/\lambda\). The mixed model uses both finite inputs. Then

\[x_s=\tfrac32F^2\lambda(\lambda/V)^2\ell D.\]

For a Gaussian distribution,

\[a_s=0.58+0.48c+0.24c^2,\quad b_s=0.02-0.025c,\quad y_s=Y(x_s;a_s,b_s,2.12).\]

For a Lorentzian distribution,

\[a_s=0.025+0.285c,\qquad b_s=\begin{cases}0.15-0.2(0.75-c)^2,&c>0,\\-0.45c,&c\le0,\end{cases}\qquad y_s=Y(x_s;a_s,b_s,2).\]

Type I uses \(y=y_s\). Type II and mixed use \(y=y_p y_s\). The implemented identity/degenerate limits must be retained when evaluating zero radii, zero spread or vanishing angle factors; do not manufacture infinities by cancelling terms outside their valid domain.

items.title: Larson factors
items.text:
For the isotropic coefficient \(x\),

\[y=\left[1+0.001\,xF^2\lambda^3/\sin2\theta\right]^{-1/2}.\]

For the anisotropic form,

\[x_{\rm aniso}=x_{11}h^2+x_{22}k^2+x_{33}l^2+x_{12}hk+x_{13}hl+x_{23}kl,\qquad x_{\rm eff}=\frac{x_{\rm aniso}}{4(\sin\theta/\lambda)^2},\]

and substitute \(x_{\rm eff}\) for \(x\) in the same intensity factor. The cross coefficients are entered in the polynomial as written, without an additional factor of two. The implementation returns the identity at vanishing \(\sin2\theta\) or a nonpositive empirical radicand; such a result is not evidence for a physically justified coefficient choice.

items.title: Applicability
items.text: These are spherical/isotropic Becker–Coppens approximations and the stated empirical Larson forms, not a general dynamical-diffraction solution. Parameter values can be correlated with scale and structure; inspect the strong-reflection residuals and the reliability factors.

items.title: References
items.text:
1. Becker, P. J. & Coppens, P. (1974). Acta Crystallographica A, 30, 129–147. DOI. Extinction theory and spherical approximations.
  2. Becker, P. J. & Coppens, P. (1974). Acta Crystallographica A, 30, 148–153. Application of the extinction treatment.
  3. Larson extinction convention, as used in SHELXL and the Mag2Pol manual, §5.1.3. The operative intensity factor and units for this reference are stated above.

items.title: Lorentz and polarization factors
items.text: These terms convert structure-factor contributions into the intensity convention of a measurement. They depend on geometry and radiation, not on a single universal powder formula.

items.title: Constant-wavelength powder Lorentz factor
items.text:
\[L_{\rm CW}(\theta)=\frac{1}{\sin\theta\sin2\theta}=\frac{1}{2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta}.\]

Evaluate it once at the reflection's Bragg angle. It does not contain the TOF \(d^4\) factor. Reflection multiplicity and the experiment's intensity-unit convention enter the intensity assembly separately.

items.title: Time-of-flight powder factor
items.text:
The fixed-bank spacing dependence is

\[L_{\rm TOF}(d)\propto d^4\sin\theta_{\rm bank}.\]

\(\theta_{\rm bank}\) is half the bank's scattering angle. Wavelength-dependent absorption uses \(\lambda=2d\sin\theta_{\rm bank}\). The full calculation retains its scattering-length/intensity unit conversion and scale; the proportionality above isolates the Lorentz dependence rather than specifying an arbitrary absolute normalisation.

items.title: X-ray polarization
items.text:
\[P=1-K+K\cos^2(2\theta_m)\cos^2(2\theta).\]

\(K\) is setup_polarization_coefficient, and the entered monochromator take-off angle setup_monochromator_twotheta is \(2\theta_m\) in degrees. At \(K=0\) the factor is unity. Apply the angle conversion before evaluating the cosines; a stored monochromator angle is not a precomputed squared cosine.

items.title: Wavelength doublet
items.text: A CW X-ray experiment may declare a second wavelength and its intensity ratio. The calculated pattern combines the two line systems with the declared weights, placing each at its own Bragg positions. It is distinct from increasing the peak width or changing the atomic displacement parameter. See calibration and the instrument parameters.

items.title: Scope
items.text: The factors here are for the stated powder geometries. They should not be copied onto a single-crystal reflection list that is already reduced to its own integrated-intensity convention. The Rietveld model shows where they enter a powder calculation.

items.title: Preferred orientation
items.text: A powder with preferred crystallite orientations does not produce the same relative reflection intensities as an ideally random powder. The supported CW model is the March–Dollase correction, with an optional random fraction.

items.title: March–Dollase factor
items.text:
\[O(h)=f+(1-f)\left\langle\left[r^2\cos^2\alpha+\frac{\sin^2\alpha}{r}\right]^{-3/2}\right\rangle.\]

\(r>0\) is march_r; \(f\) is march_random_fract. \(r=1\) or \(f=1\) gives the untextured factor. The angle \(\alpha\) is between the reflection and the declared texture axis, both treated as reciprocal-lattice vectors. The average is over the space group's point-group images of the reflection.

items.title: Axis and metric
items.text:
For reciprocal vectors \(\mathbf h\) and \(\mathbf a\),

\[\cos^2\alpha=\frac{(\mathbf h^{\mathsf T}G^*\mathbf a)^2}{(\mathbf h^{\mathsf T}G^*\mathbf h)(\mathbf a^{\mathsf T}G^*\mathbf a)}.\]

The reciprocal metric matters for non-orthogonal cells. A bare Cartesian dot product of the Miller-index triplets is not the general expression.

items.title: Scope and interpretation
items.text: A preferred-orientation row belongs to a linked structure in a CW experiment. It changes reflection intensities rather than peak positions. The implementation applies no extra volume normalisation to this factor. This model is not an arbitrary orientation-distribution function or a model for every texture geometry.

items.title: References
items.text: 1. Dollase, W. A. (1986). Correction of intensities for preferred orientation in powder diffractometry: application of the March model. Journal of Applied Crystallography, 19, 267–272.
