items.title: Peak profiles
items.text:
A profile turns an integrated reflection contribution into intensity over a powder-pattern axis. Its width and asymmetry are part of the experiment model.

  • Constant wavelength: Gaussian, Lorentzian, direct pseudo-Voigt, TCH, Bérar–Baldinozzi and Finger–Cox–Jephcoat.
  • Time of flight: symmetric pseudo-Voigt, Jorgensen and Jorgensen–Von Dreele.

The catalogue lists the exact supported type tokens. A similarly named type from another program is not sufficient to establish matching width, mixing or asymmetry conventions.

items.title: Width and normalisation
items.text: A unit-area profile integrates to one over its complete mathematical domain. Peak height therefore changes as width changes, even when integrated intensity remains fixed. FWHM \(H\) and Gaussian standard deviation \(\sigma\) satisfy \(H=\sqrt{8\ln2}\,\sigma\).

items.title: Finite peak windows
items.text: The evaluated pattern can use a finite window set by a cutoff in FWHM units. Tails outside that window are omitted; a finite window is a calculation choice rather than a new physical profile. The current window extent is cutoff_fwhm * H; a nonpositive cutoff selects the full-range path. Keep the cutoff when comparing calculations, particularly for Lorentzian tails.

items.title: Constant-wavelength peak profiles
items.text: Use \(\Delta=2\theta-2\theta_h\) and FWHM \(H\) in degrees. Widths, mixing and the production asymmetry coefficients are evaluated at the reflection's Bragg angle, not independently at every sampled pattern point.

items.title: Symmetric primitives
items.text:
\[G(\Delta;H)=\frac{2}{H}\sqrt{\frac{\ln2}{\pi}}\exp[-4\ln2(\Delta/H)^2],\qquad L(\Delta;H)=\frac{2}{\pi H}\frac{1}{1+4(\Delta/H)^2}.\] \[pV(\Delta;H,\eta)=(1-\eta)G(\Delta;H)+\eta L(\Delta;H).\]

Both components use the same \(H\). cwl-gaussian uses \(\eta=0\) and cwl-lorentzian uses \(\eta=1\).

items.title: Direct width and mixing
items.text:
For Gaussian, Lorentzian and direct pseudo-Voigt types,

\[H^2=U\tan^2\theta+V\tan\theta+W.\]

cwl-pseudo-voigt additionally uses \(\eta=\eta_0+\eta_1(2\theta)\) with \(2\theta\) in degrees. mixing_eta_1 is therefore per degree. An unphysical width or mixing choice is not repaired by interpreting the parameters as a different profile type.

items.title: Thompson–Cox–Hastings
items.text:
cwl-tch-pseudo-voigt derives a combined width and mixing from

\[H_G^2=U\tan^2\theta+V\tan\theta+W,\qquad H_L=X\tan\theta+Y/\cos\theta.\] \[\begin{aligned} H^5={}&H_G^5+2.69269H_G^4H_L+2.42843H_G^3H_L^2\\ &+4.47163H_G^2H_L^3+0.07842H_GH_L^4+H_L^5,\\ \eta={}&1.36603r-0.47719r^2+0.11116r^3,\qquad r=H_L/H. \end{aligned}\]

\(U,V,W\) have degree-squared units; \(X,Y\) have degree units. Here X multiplies \(\tan\theta\) and Y multiplies \(1/\cos\theta\). The implementation's nonnegative TCH mixing floor is zero, preserving the Gaussian endpoint. The combined \(H\) is used by both Gaussian and Lorentzian components.

items.title: Bérar–Baldinozzi asymmetry
items.text:
cwl-pseudo-voigt-berar-baldinozzi applies the direct pseudo-Voigt width/mixing with an empirical multiplicative factor. Let \(z=\Delta/H\):

\[F_a(z)=2ze^{-z^2},\qquad F_b(z)=2(2z^2-3)F_a(z),\] \[A(\theta)=A_0/\tan\theta+A_1/\tan2\theta,\qquad B(\theta)=B_0/\tan\theta+B_1/\tan2\theta,\] \[\Omega(\Delta)=pV(\Delta)[1+A(\theta)F_a(z)+B(\theta)F_b(z)].\]

Parameters are asym_beba_a0, asym_beba_b0, asym_beba_a1, asym_beba_b1 and the limit angle asym_beba_limit. At or above that limit in degrees \(2\theta\), the asymmetry correction is omitted. It is a descriptor, not an independent free fit parameter. The production per-reflection evaluation keeps the odd factor centred on each reflection.

items.title: Finger–Cox–Jephcoat asymmetry
items.text:
cwl-tch-pseudo-voigt-fcj convolves the TCH core with an axial-divergence weight. Put \(S_L=S/L\) and \(D_L=D/L\), half the sample and detector heights divided by the diffractometer radius:

\[\cos2\phi_{\min}=\cos2\theta_h\sqrt{1+(S_L+D_L)^2},\qquad \cos2\phi_{\rm infl}=\cos2\theta_h\sqrt{1+(S_L-D_L)^2}.\]

With \(q(\delta)=|\cos2\theta_h|/\sqrt{\cos^2\delta-\cos^22\theta_h}\), the two geometric regions use

\[G(\delta)=\begin{cases}\left|[(S_L+D_L)q(\delta)-1]/\cos\delta\right|,&\text{inner region},\\ 2\min(S_L,D_L)q(\delta)/\cos\delta,&\text{outer region}. \end{cases}\]

Integrate between \(2\phi_{\min}\) and \(2\theta_h\). The inner branch applies when \(|\delta-2\phi_{\min}|\le|2\phi_{\rm infl}-2\phi_{\min}|\); the outer branch applies beyond that boundary. The normalised quadrature is

\[\Omega(x)=\frac{\sum_k w_kG(\delta_k)\,pV(x-\delta_k+2\theta_h)}{\sum_k w_kG(\delta_k)}.\]

asym_fcj_1 is \(S_L\) and asym_fcj_2 is \(D_L\). The implementation handles zero/equal-height limits and uses the symmetric profile within 0.4° of \(2\theta_h=90°\); these evaluation conventions are part of the model, not new free parameters.

items.title: References
items.text:
1. Caglioti, G., Paoletti, A. & Ricci, F. P. (1958). Nuclear Instruments, 3, 223–228. Angular dependence of peak widths.
  2. Thompson, P., Cox, D. E. & Hastings, J. B. (1987). Journal of Applied Crystallography, 20, 79–83. DOI. TCH width and mixing.
  3. Bérar, J.-F. & Baldinozzi, G. (1993). Journal of Applied Crystallography, 26, 128–129. Empirical profile asymmetry.
  4. Finger, L. W., Cox, D. E. & Jephcoat, A. P. (1994). Journal of Applied Crystallography, 27, 892–900. Axial-divergence asymmetry.

items.title: Time-of-flight peak profiles
items.text: Let \(\delta=t-t_h\) in microseconds. The bank geometry supplies the wavelength of each reflection; calibration maps spacing to the peak centre.

items.title: Gaussian and Lorentzian width terms
items.text:
\[\sigma_G^2(d)=v_0+(v_1+\mathrm{strain}_G)d^2+(v_2+\mathrm{size}_G)d^4,\] \[H_G=\sqrt{8\ln2}\,\sigma_G,\qquad H_L(d)=\gamma_0+(\gamma_1+\mathrm{strain}_L)d+(\gamma_2+\mathrm{size}_L)d^2.\]

Here \(v_0,v_1,v_2\) denote the stored variance coefficients labelled σ₀², σ₁² and σ₂²; the superscript is part of the variance notation, not an instruction to square their stored values again. The broad_gauss_sigma_* coefficients are variance coefficients, not standard deviations or FWHMs. broad_lorentz_gamma_* coefficients define Lorentzian FWHM. Keep their respective time/spacing units; see the parameter index.

items.title: Symmetric pseudo-Voigt
items.text: tof-pseudo-voigt uses the TCH width/mixing, with \(H_G,H_L\) in microseconds, and the symmetric unit-area pseudo-Voigt. It does not add the back-to-back exponential pulse.

items.title: Jorgensen pulse and profile
items.text:
tof-jorgensen convolves a two-sided exponential pulse with a Gaussian. The rates are

\[\alpha(d)=\alpha_0+\alpha_1/d,\qquad \beta(d)=\beta_0+\beta_1/d^4,\]

with positive evaluated rates in inverse microseconds. Let \(N=\alpha\beta/[2(\alpha+\beta)]\) and \(\sigma\) be the Gaussian standard deviation:

\[\Omega_G(\delta)=N[e^u\operatorname{erfc}(y)+e^v\operatorname{erfc}(z)],\] \[\begin{aligned} u&=\tfrac12\alpha(\alpha\sigma^2+2\delta),& y&=(\alpha\sigma^2+\delta)/(\sqrt2\sigma),\\ v&=\tfrac12\beta(\beta\sigma^2-2\delta),& z&=(\beta\sigma^2-\delta)/(\sqrt2\sigma). \end{aligned}\]

The normalisation already includes the Gaussian-convolution factors; do not reuse \(N\) as if it alone normalised a bare piecewise exponential. The numerical evaluation uses stable exponential/error-function combinations to avoid overflow without changing this equation.

items.title: Jorgensen–Von Dreele
items.text:
tof-jorgensen-von-dreele adds the Lorentzian contribution through a common TCH width \(H\) and mixing \(\eta\):

\[\Omega=(1-\eta)\Omega_G+\eta\Omega_L.\]

Both terms use that combined width: \(\sigma=H/\sqrt{8\ln2}\) in \(\Omega_G\) and FWHM \(H\) in \(\Omega_L\).

\[\Omega_L=-\frac{2N}{\pi}\left(\operatorname{Im}[e^pE_1(p)]+\operatorname{Im}[e^qE_1(q)]\right),\] \[p=\alpha\delta+i\alpha H/2,\qquad q=-\beta\delta+i\beta H/2.\]

\(E_1\) is the exponential integral. At zero Lorentzian width the profile reduces to its Gaussian Jorgensen limit; assigning a different width to each mixed kernel would define a different model.

items.title: Ikeda–Carpenter
items.text: Planned. Ikeda–Carpenter is planned for TOF pulse modelling. It is not a selectable profile in this reference snapshot. See Time-of-flight peak profiles for the availability of this and the implemented profiles.

items.title: References
items.text:
1. Von Dreele, R. B., Jorgensen, J. D. & Windsor, C. G. (1982). Journal of Applied Crystallography, 15, 581–589. Time-of-flight profile modelling.
  2. Thompson, P., Cox, D. E. & Hastings, J. B. (1987). Journal of Applied Crystallography, 20, 79–83. DOI. Width and mixing convention.

items.title: Start here
items.text: Work with Python objects in scripts and notebooks, with direct access to parameters, data arrays and results.

items.title: Set up Python
items.text:
Install the easydiffraction package in a Python environment.

Set up Python

items.title: Scripts and notebooks
items.text:
EasyDiffraction in a Jupyter notebook

Both use the same Python API:

  • Python scripts combine edi with your own data preparation and analysis tools.
  • Jupyter notebooks run code one cell at a time and keep plots and results beside it.

To try it, download the example notebook and the example project it opens.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Run a notebook tutorial.
  • Look up a call in the Python quick reference.

items.title: Calculate a pattern
items.text: A calculation predicts the data from the current model. It does not optimize the model parameters. Use it for a simulation, or to inspect the starting model before a fit.

items.title: Calculate the loaded project
items.text:
import edi

project = edi.Project.load('path/to/project')
project.analysis.calculate()

The calculation reads its structures, experiments and settings from the project. You do not pass a second grid or measurement alongside it.

items.title: Inspect calculated powder intensities
items.text:
for experiment in project.experiments:
    if experiment.data is not None:
        calculated = experiment.data.intensity_calc
        print(experiment.name, len(calculated), 'calculated points')

calculate() returns no result object. The calculated data is stored on each experiment. The example above covers the powder-pattern view; single-crystal experiments use reflection data instead.

items.title: Calculate without measured data
items.text:
A complete simulation project declares an axis range in its experiment file. The catalogue's powder simulation is pd-neut-cwl_lbco_simulation; its tutorial calculates from the model and inspects the experiment's calculated intensities.

The absence of observations is expected for a simulation. It also means there is no measured pattern to fit against.

items.title: Save or present the result
items.text:
project.save_as('calculated-project')
project.report.save_html('calculation.html', offline=True)

Saving and reporting are explicit choices. A report is a presentation of the project; keep the editable project when you want to continue the analysis later.

items.title: Get data and tutorials
items.text: EasyDiffraction keeps its example structures, measured data and projects in one collection, the same one the application's Load ▾ From web… reads. Python lists it and downloads what you name.

items.title: List and download data
items.text:
import edi

edi.list_data()  # every entry, numbered
edi.list_data('project')  # one kind: structure, experiment, data or project
path = edi.download_data('pd-neut-cwl_lbco-hrpt', destination='data')

download_data takes an entry's id, or its number in the last listing. Use the id in saved code, since numbers follow the listing. It returns the downloaded file. A project archive is unpacked into a folder named after the entry and its digest, and that folder is returned, ready for edi.Project.load. Every file's size and SHA-256 are checked against the collection's index, and a mismatch is refused. A file already downloaded and still matching is kept unless you pass overwrite=True.

The collection is read from GitHub, with data.easydiffraction.org as the mirror when GitHub cannot be reached. Set EDI_COLLECTION to a folder or URL, or pass source=, to read another collection.

items.title: List and download tutorials
items.text:
edi.list_tutorials()
edi.download_tutorial('pd-neut-cwl_lbco-hrpt', destination='tutorials')
edi.download_tutorial(1, file_format='py')
edi.download_all_tutorials(destination='tutorials')

Tutorials come as Jupyter notebooks (ipynb, the default) or Python scripts (py), listed in their learning order. Each one's first cell installs edi and gets its data.

items.title: Experiments and data
items.text:
An experiment describes the measurement and the model used to calculate it. For powder diffraction, that includes instrument and peak-profile settings, background, exclusions and linked structures.

The shared Experiment chapter explains the scientific model; the steps below describe this interface.

items.title: Inspect a project
items.text:
import edi

project = edi.Project.load('path/to/project')

for experiment in project.experiments:
    print(experiment.name)

Keep experimental settings with the measurement they describe. Structural parameters belong to a structure, while wavelength and zero shift and profile parameters belong to the experiment model.

items.title: Read a measured powder pattern
items.text:
For a loaded powder experiment, its data exposes measured intensities and their uncertainties. After a calculation it also carries the calculated intensities:

project.analysis.calculate()

for experiment in project.experiments:
    pattern = experiment.data
    if pattern is not None:
        print(experiment.name, len(pattern.intensity_calc))

This snippet is limited to the powder-pattern data view. Single-crystal experiments carry reflections and require the corresponding reflection API.

items.title: Construct an experiment from a data file
items.text:
For a constant-wavelength neutron powder measurement:

experiment = edi.ExperimentFactory.from_data_path(
    name='measurement',
    data_path='measurement.xye',
    sample_form='powder',
    beam_mode='constant wavelength',
    radiation_probe='neutron',
)

The powder reader accepts plain x y or x y sigma rows, separated by whitespace or commas. It skips nonnumeric lines, estimates uncertainty when omitted, drops nonpositive intensities, sorts the axis and keeps the first repeated-axis point. Review the resulting data when converting an unfamiliar file.

The factory creates the experiment and reads its data. You still need to choose its instrument/profile settings and link a structure before treating it as a complete model.

items.title: Read an experiment from CIF
items.text:
experiment = edi.ExperimentFactory.from_cif_path('experiment.cif')
project.experiments.add_from_cif_path('experiment.cif')

Both read a CIF or .edi file with the experiment's type, instrument, peak profile, background, excluded regions, linked structures and measured points. from_cif_str and add_from_cif_str take the text instead. An experiment added to a project must link structures the project holds; otherwise the import is refused and the project is left as it was. Imported values start fixed, and items EasyDiffraction does not read come back as warnings. See CIF files.

experiment.instrument.facility and experiment.instrument.name say where the measurement was made, ? when unknown. experiment.experiment_type.dimensionality is 1d, and experiment.experiment_type.polarisation is unpolarised for neutrons and . for X-rays; each accepts only that value.

items.title: Measured data or a simulation range
items.text:
A measured pattern supports comparison and fitting. A simulation range supports a forward calculation without observations. A project can contain both kinds; fitting uses experiments with measured data.

Read calculate a pattern or load and fit for the next step.

items.title: Load and fit a project
items.text: Start from a complete project with measured data. It contains the structures, experiments, free parameters and analysis settings that determine the fit.

items.title: Load
items.text:
import edi

project = edi.Project.load('path/to/project')

The input may be a project folder, its project.edi, or a project .zip. Invalid or incomplete input raises edi.IoError rather than returning a partially loaded project. Project loading explains what the loader checks.

items.title: Inspect the free parameters
items.text:
for parameter in project.free_parameters:
    print(parameter.name, parameter.value, parameter.units)

The project already declares which parameters may vary. Review that choice before fitting; structures and parameters shows how a model parameter exposes its value and free flag.

items.title: Fit
items.text:
result = project.analysis.fit()
print(result.rwp)
print(result.reduced_chi_square)

analysis.fit() dispatches according to the fitting mode saved in the project. The shared fitting-mode guide explains the modes and their starting-state policies; the same method runs each declared mode. Scan results have a different shape from single or joint outcomes: use result handling.

items.title: Follow progress
items.text:
For a single or joint fit, an optional callback receives each iteration record:

def show_iteration(record):
    print(record)


result = project.analysis.fit(on_iteration=show_iteration)

The facade also supports on_start, scan-specific on_scan_start and on_file_complete, and a should_cancel predicate. Scan callbacks are accepted only for a scan-mode project. These hooks report progress; the model and measured data remain in the project.

items.title: Read the result
items.text: For a powder single or joint fit, inspect Rwp and reduced χ² alongside the pattern, uncertainties and correlations. Read the result explains the returned values. A finished minimization alone does not establish that the structural model is appropriate.

items.title: Prepare a report
items.text: project.report.save_html('result.html')

items.title: Save the updated project
items.text:
project.save_as('fitted-project')

save_as() puts the project in the new folder and makes that its location for later saves. A Python single or joint fit does not automatically save your project. Scan analysis also writes its progress results during the run; retain the input project separately when you need its initial state.

Open the saved result in the application to inspect it visually, or run the project through the Command line.

items.title: Load and save projects
items.text: A complete project brings together structures, experiments, measured data or a calculation range, and analysis settings. Python opens the same saved projects as the application and Command line.

items.title: Open a project
items.text:
import edi

project = edi.Project.load('path/to/project')

The same loader accepts a project entry file or a zip archive:

project = edi.Project.load('path/to/project/project.edi')
project = edi.Project.load('project.zip')

Each statement opens a project; choose the input form you have. A project.edi refers to the complete project beside it, rather than being a standalone replacement for all its files.

items.title: What a successful load means
items.text:
The loader checks the project as a whole. Experiment links must resolve to the project's structures. A powder experiment declares either observed data with uncertainties or a simulation range. An incomplete, ambiguous or invalid input raises edi.IoError instead of returning a partially populated project.

try:
    project = edi.Project.load('path/to/project')
except edi.IoError as error:
    print(error)

items.title: Inspect its contents
items.text:
print(project.metadata.title)
print(project.location)
print([structure.name for structure in project.structures])
print([experiment.name for experiment in project.experiments])
print(project.analysis.fitting_mode)

Collections expose the current model. A complete project can hold several structures and experiments; it is not restricted to one crystal model and one bank.

items.title: Save or move the project
items.text:
project.save()
project.save_as('fitted-project')

save() writes to the project's current location. When Python opened a zip, project.location is the zip path and save() rewrites that archive. save_as(folder) writes to a folder and makes it the location for subsequent saves.

Saving rounds values to their output precision and recalculates the displayed model from the saved values. Small numerical changes after a save can therefore reflect the precision of the persisted project.

items.title: Hand on an archive
items.text:
project.save()
project.export_zip('shared-project.zip')

export_zip() packages the project's folder as last saved. Save first when you want current in-memory changes included. The exported archive can be opened by the other interfaces.

Read shared data formats for the project structure and Command line files and output for the different archive write-back rule used by commands.

items.title: Python quick reference
items.text: This page covers the calls used in the Python guides. It is a selected reference, not a complete generated API catalogue. The current declared surface lists the broader interface; signatures and behavior should be checked in the matching edi version.

items.title: Project input and output
items.text: Call or property Purpose edi.Project.load(path) Open a complete project folder, its project.edi, or a zip. project.location Read the project's current location. project.save() Write the project to its current location. project.save_as(folder) Write a folder and continue working there. project.export_zip(path) Package the project's folder as last saved.

items.title: Model inspection
items.text:
Property Purpose project.structures Inspect the project's structures. project.experiments Inspect its experiments. project.free_parameters Inspect parameters whose free flag is set. parameter.value Read or change a parameter's value. parameter.free Read or change whether it may vary. Freeing a value a fit cannot vary raises an error with the reason.

Factories used here are StructureFactory.from_cif_path(path), ExperimentFactory.from_cif_path(path) and ExperimentFactory.from_data_path(...). These create model components, not automatically complete analysis projects. project.structures.add_from_cif_path(path) and project.experiments.add_from_cif_path(path) read a CIF or .edi file and add the result to the project; each reader also has a _str form that takes text.

items.title: Analysis
items.text:
Call or property Purpose project.analysis.calculate() Calculate from the current project; results stay on experiments. project.analysis.fit() Run the fit selected by the declared mode. project.analysis.fitting_mode Read or set single, joint, sequential or independent. project.analysis.descent Read or select a registered descent strategy.

Optional fit callbacks are on_start, on_iteration, on_scan_start, on_file_complete and should_cancel. Scan-specific callbacks require a scan-mode project.

items.title: Reports
items.text:
Call Purpose project.report.as_html(...) Obtain HTML text. project.report.save_html(path, ...) Write an HTML report. project.report.save(...) Write the selected formats except PDF, which the application writes. project.report.save_cif(path) Write a CIF report. project.report.check() Read saved-report freshness states.

See reports for call-specific options and the difference between saved settings and per-call overrides.

items.title: Reports from Python
items.text:
The project's report brings together structures, experiments, calculated patterns and fit information. The application, Python and Command line use the same report model and saved settings.

The shared Report chapter explains the scientific model; the steps below describe this interface.

items.title: Save interactive HTML
items.text:
html_path = project.report.save_html('fit-report.html', offline=True)
print(html_path)

offline=True embeds the chart libraries, so the report does not need to fetch them when opened. With online libraries, a smaller report loads those libraries from the web. Charts remain interactive in HTML.

items.title: Display in a notebook
items.text:
project.report

The report's notebook representation shows the document. To obtain its HTML text explicitly:

html = project.report.as_html(offline=True)

items.title: Choose contents for one call
items.text:
project.report.save_html(
    'fit-report.html',
    offline=True,
    x_axis='d_spacing',
    excluded=['data'],
)

native and d_spacing select the pattern axis. Optional exclusions use charts, correlations, reflections, data and evolution. Keyword overrides affect that call; they do not overwrite the project's saved settings.

items.title: Save the selected report formats
items.text:
written = project.report.save()
states = project.report.check()
print(written)
print(states)

save() writes the formats selected by the project except PDF, which is written by the application. check() returns saved report names with current, out of date or missing states.

Saving a project is separate from saving a report. A later model or report-settings change can make an existing report out of date.

items.title: Supported outputs
items.text:
HTML is available from Python, including self-contained offline HTML. PDF is written by the application.

cif_path = project.report.save_cif()

save_cif() writes the CIF report, by default to reports/<name>.cif in the project folder. It holds the fit result, then one data block for each structure and each experiment. Every item is written under its official CIF name, or an _edi_ name where CIF has none, with its standard uncertainty.

Keep the complete Edi project as the editable analysis record.

items.title: Read the result
items.text: Inspect the pattern, parameter values and uncertainties together. Agreement factors summarize a fit; they do not replace a scientific assessment of the model.

items.title: Summary and status
items.text:
For a single or joint powder fit:

result = project.analysis.fit()

print(result.status.name)
print(result.iterations)
print(result.rwp)
print(result.reduced_chi_square)

Check the status before interpreting a result as converged. Rwp and reduced χ² depend on the data, uncertainties, fitted range and free parameters. See fit quality for the shared interpretation.

items.title: Values and uncertainties
items.text:
The single/joint fit result exposes labelled parameter values and their uncertainties:

for label, value in result.values.items():
    uncertainty = result.uncertainty.get(label)
    print(label, value, uncertainty)

An absent uncertainty is kept as None in this example; it is not replaced with zero. A small numerical uncertainty should still be considered alongside the model's assumptions and parameter correlations.

items.title: Several banks
items.text:
for bank in result.banks:
    print(bank.name, bank.rwp)

Per-bank information helps identify a mismatch hidden by a combined summary.

items.title: Scan results
items.text: Sequential and independent modes produce one record per measured file and keep scan progress under analysis/. Use the scan's result table and the report's evolution view to follow changing parameters. The single/joint snippets above are not a complete scan-result reference.

items.title: Save evidence with the model
items.text: Prepare an interactive report for inspection and save the project when you want the fitted values to persist. Reopening the project provides the editable model behind the report.

items.title: Set up Python
items.text: Install the easydiffraction distribution and import it as edi. The same installation works in scripts, notebooks, and with python -m edi.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Use CPython 3.12 or newer on macOS with Apple Silicon or Linux x86-64; Windows follows in a later release. The package comes from the v2026.11.8 release on GitHub; its dependencies come from PyPI.

PixiPython + pip

Create a project and install Python:

pixi init edi-python
cd edi-python
pixi add "python>=3.12"

In pixi.toml, add the EasyDiffraction package index:

[pypi-options]
extra-index-urls = ["https://download.easydiffraction.org/pypi/simple/"]

Then add the package and check it:

pixi add --pypi "easydiffraction==2026.11.8"
pixi run python -c "import easydiffraction as edi; print(edi.Project)"
pixi run python -m edi --help

To upgrade, run the same pixi add with the new release's version.

Create a virtual environment:

python -m venv .venv

Activate it with source .venv/bin/activate on macOS or Linux, or .\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 in Windows PowerShell. Then install and check:

python -m pip install "easydiffraction==2026.11.8" --extra-index-url https://download.easydiffraction.org/pypi/simple/
python -c "import easydiffraction as edi; print(edi.Project)"
python -m edi --help

To upgrade, run the install command again with the new release's version.

items.title: In a notebook
items.text:
Install and launch JupyterLab from the environment where you installed edi.

PixiPython + pip 
pixi add jupyterlab
pixi run jupyter lab

python -m pip install jupyterlab
python -m jupyterlab

Select the kernel for that environment when you open a notebook.

Run an example

items.title: Structures and parameters
items.text:
A structure describes the crystal: its symmetry, unit-cell geometry and atom sites. Experiments link the structures that contribute to their calculated data.

The shared Structure chapter explains the scientific model; the steps below describe this interface.

items.title: Inspect a loaded structure
items.text:
import edi

project = edi.Project.load('path/to/project')

for structure in project.structures:
    print(structure.name)
    print(structure.space_group.name_h_m)
    print(structure.cell.length_a.value)

Cell lengths and angles are parameters with values. A space-group name selects symmetry; it is not a floating-point fit parameter.

items.title: Read and change a parameter
items.text:
For a project with at least one structure:

structure = project.structures[0]
length_a = structure.cell.length_a

print(length_a.value)
print(length_a.free)
length_a.free = True

The free flag allows a parameter to vary during a fit. Set it only when that parameter belongs in the scientific model you intend to fit. Setting free = True on a value a fit cannot vary raises an error that gives the reason. On a value set by symmetry or a constraint, it is ignored with a warning and the value stays dependent. Shared parameter concepts explain values, uncertainties and constraints.

items.title: Inspect the free set
items.text:
for parameter in project.free_parameters:
    print(parameter.name, parameter.value, parameter.units)

This project-level list includes structural and experimental parameters. It helps you review the analysis before running a fit.

items.title: Read a structure file
items.text:
The factory reads a structure from a CIF or .edi file, and the project's collection reads one and adds it:

structure = edi.StructureFactory.from_cif_path('structure.cif')
project.structures.add_from_cif_path('structure.cif')

from_cif_str and add_from_cif_str take the text instead of a path.

This creates a structure object; it does not by itself create a complete measurement and analysis project. Imported values start fixed. Items in the file that EasyDiffraction does not read come back as Python warnings starting with crysta.schema.cif_items_not_read, and a file EasyDiffraction cannot read raises an error that names the item. See CIF files.

For a complete runnable analysis, start from a project or a checked example. These pages intentionally document a demonstrated subset rather than claiming that all constructors and file variants are covered.

Compare Python paths with GUI labels, Edi keys and CIF names.

items.title: Analysis workflow
items.text:
Follow these stages with the edi Python API.

  1. Project
  2. Structure
  3. Experiment
  4. Analysis
  5. Report
Stage In Python Project Load and save a project Structure Read and change structures and their parameters Experiment Work with experiments and their data Analysis Calculate a pattern, fit a project and inspect the results Report Generate and save a report

The shared analysis workflow explains the science behind each stage.

items.title: Fit with your own AI assistant
items.text: ChatGPT or Claude, in their desktop apps or command-line tools, can write a Jupyter notebook that fits a structure with EasyDiffraction. This page gives a prompt for the La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ example of the La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ on HRPT tutorial. The prompt links the documentation and the notebook tutorials, so the assistant can read how EasyDiffraction is used, and it names the fit stages, so the notebook fits in the same order as the tutorial.

items.title: Get the two files
items.text:
Download the structure and the measured pattern from EasyDiffraction's collection into one folder:

  • tutorial-lbco.cif: the cubic perovskite, La and Ba sharing the corner site.
  • tutorial-hrpt.xye: the HRPT pattern, 2θ in degrees, the counts and their standard uncertainties.

items.title: Ask for the notebook
items.text:
Start the assistant in that folder, or attach the two files to the chat, and give it this prompt:

Fit the crystal structure of La0.5Ba0.5CoO3 to neutron powder diffraction data with
EasyDiffraction (edi).

Documentation: https://easydiffraction.org/ (a short index for assistants:
https://easydiffraction.org/llms.txt).
Worked examples: https://easydiffraction.org/python/tutorials/ (choose the one closest to this task).

The two input files are in this folder:
- tutorial-lbco.cif: the structure, space group P m -3 m, La and Ba sharing one site.
- tutorial-hrpt.xye: the measured pattern, constant-wavelength neutrons on HRPT at PSI, wavelength
  1.494 Å; columns 2θ (degrees), counts and their standard uncertainties.

Create a Jupyter notebook, ready to run, that loads both files and fits the structure in stages.
Each stage frees one more group of parameters and keeps the ones freed before it free:
1. the scale, the 2θ zero and the cell length a;
2. the background points;
3. the peak widths U, V, W and Y;
4. the isotropic displacements (B iso) of La, Ba, Co and O.
After stage 4, show the correlations. La's and Ba's B iso should move together almost exactly.
Constrain Ba's B iso to equal La's, and fit again.

After every fit, show the fitted parameters. At the end, give the reduced χ², Rwp and each fitted
value with its standard uncertainty.

The notebook it returns should run from top to bottom in an environment with EasyDiffraction installed (see Setup). Compare its final values with the La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ on HRPT tutorial's: an assistant can pick other starting values or miss a step, and the tutorial shows what each stage should give.

The same prompt, asking for a project for edi fit, is on the Command line tutorials. The application has an AI assistant built in.

items.text: Google Colab Open in Google Colab Download Notebook

items.title: Co₂SiO₄ on D20
items.text: This tutorial fits the olivine Co₂SiO₄ to constant-wavelength neutron powder data measured on D20 at the ILL. Its structure and its measured pattern come from EasyDiffraction's collection; the tutorial describes the experiment, links the two and fits the coordinates, the displacements and the oxygen occupancies.

items.title: Import the library
items.text: import easydiffraction as edi

items.title: Define the project
items.text: project = edi.Project(name='cosio_d20')

items.title: Define the structure
items.text:
Load the structure from the collection. The CIF gives the space group P n m a, the cell and the six sites, and marks the cell, coordinates, displacements and oxygen occupancies to fit. The fit below frees them in stages, so start with all of them fixed.

structure_path = edi.download_data('pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20-cosio', destination='data')
project.structures.add_from_cif_path(structure_path)
structure = project.structures['cosio']
for parameter in project.free_parameters:
    parameter.free = False

Data 'pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20-cosio' is at data/pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20-cosio.edi

project.display.structure('cosio')

items.title: Define the experiment
items.text:
The measured pattern also comes from the collection.

data_path = edi.download_data('pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20-d20-data', destination='data')
project.experiments.add_from_data_path(
    name='d20',
    data_path=data_path,
    sample_form='powder',
    beam_mode='constant wavelength',
    radiation_probe='neutron',
    scattering_type='bragg',
)
experiment = project.experiments['d20']

Data 'pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20-d20-data' is at data/pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20-d20.xye

D20's wavelength is 1.87 Å. The profile is the Thompson-Cox-Hastings pseudo-Voigt, and a flat background runs through fourteen points.

experiment.instrument.setup_wavelength = 1.87
experiment.instrument.calib_twotheta_offset = 0
experiment.peak.broad_gauss_u = 0.2
experiment.peak.broad_gauss_v = -0.5
experiment.peak.broad_gauss_w = 0.4
experiment.peak.broad_lorentz_y = 0.01
for position in (8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 15, 25, 30, 50, 70, 90, 110, 130, 150):
    experiment.background.create(position=position, intensity=340)
experiment.linked_structures.create(structure_id='cosio', scale=1)

project.display.pattern('d20')

items.title: Perform the analysis
items.text: The fit goes in stages, freeing one group of parameters at a time.

items.title: Scale, 2θ zero and cell
items.text:
The scale sets the overall height of the pattern, and the zero shift and the three cell lengths put the peaks where they are measured.

experiment.linked_structures['cosio'].scale.free = True
experiment.instrument.calib_twotheta_offset.free = True
structure.cell.length_a.free = True
structure.cell.length_b.free = True
structure.cell.length_c.free = True

project.display.parameters.free()

project.analysis.fit()
project.display.fit.results()

edi fit: project cosio_d20, 1418 pts fitted / 1418 loaded, 5 free
   iter   time (s)   Rwp (%)  reduced χ²   change
                       40.51       452.01
      1      0.024     20.61       117.03   74.1% ↓
      2      0.027     20.10       111.27   4.9% ↓
      3      0.030     20.09       111.14   0.1% ↓
      4      0.034     20.09       111.14   
      5      0.037     20.09       111.14   
      6      0.042     20.09       111.14   
  done · converged · 6 iters · reduced χ² 111.14 · Rwp 20.09 % · 0.05 s

project.display.pattern('d20')

items.title: Background
items.text:
With the peaks in place, the fourteen background points follow the level between them.

for point in experiment.background:
    point.intensity.free = True

project.analysis.fit()
project.display.fit.results()

edi fit: project cosio_d20, 1418 pts fitted / 1418 loaded, 19 free
   iter   time (s)   Rwp (%)  reduced χ²   change
                       20.09       112.25
      1      0.029      5.51         8.45   92.5% ↓
  done · converged · 1 iters · reduced χ² 8.45 · Rwp 5.51 % · 0.03 s

project.display.pattern('d20')

items.title: Peak widths
items.text:
The profile terms now fit the widths and shapes of the peaks. diffraction-lib's tutorial also fits a peak asymmetry; this case's profile has none.

experiment.peak.broad_gauss_u.free = True
experiment.peak.broad_gauss_v.free = True
experiment.peak.broad_gauss_w.free = True
experiment.peak.broad_lorentz_y.free = True

project.analysis.fit()
project.display.fit.results()

edi fit: project cosio_d20, 1418 pts fitted / 1418 loaded, 23 free
   iter   time (s)   Rwp (%)  reduced χ²   change
                        5.51         8.47
      1      0.032      4.80         6.42   24.2% ↓
      2      0.037      4.80         6.42   
      3      0.044      4.80         6.42   
  done · converged · 3 iters · reduced χ² 6.42 · Rwp 4.80 % · 0.05 s

project.display.pattern('d20')

items.title: Atom positions
items.text:
The peak intensities now depend mostly on where the atoms are. Co1 sits on a centre of symmetry and the other sites on the mirror plane, so only their free coordinates are fitted.

for site in structure.atom_sites:
    for coordinate in (site.fract_x, site.fract_y, site.fract_z):
        coordinate.free = not coordinate.symmetry_constrained

project.analysis.fit()
project.display.fit.results()

edi fit: project cosio_d20, 1418 pts fitted / 1418 loaded, 34 free
   iter   time (s)   Rwp (%)  reduced χ²   change
                        4.80         6.47
      1      0.040      4.14         4.82   25.5% ↓
      2      0.049      4.14         4.82   
  done · converged · 2 iters · reduced χ² 4.82 · Rwp 4.14 % · 0.06 s

project.display.pattern('d20')

items.title: Displacements
items.text:
The displacements change the intensities more at high angle.

for site in structure.atom_sites:
    site.adp_iso.free = True

project.analysis.fit()
project.display.fit.results()

edi fit: project cosio_d20, 1418 pts fitted / 1418 loaded, 40 free
   iter   time (s)   Rwp (%)  reduced χ²   change
                        4.14         4.84
      1      0.046      3.99         4.49   7.2% ↓
  done · converged · 1 iters · reduced χ² 4.49 · Rwp 3.99 % · 0.05 s

project.display.pattern('d20')

project.display.fit.correlations()

items.title: Constrain the two Co sites
items.text:
The correlations show no strong pair for the two Co sites, yet the fit gives them very different displacements, Co1's even negative, which no atom can have: both are Co and scatter alike, so the pattern cannot tell their thermal motions apart. Give each an alias and constrain Co2's to follow Co1's, starting again from 0.5 Å², then fit again; the shared displacement is positive and its s.u. smaller than either had alone.

structure.atom_sites['Co2'].adp_iso.free = False
structure.atom_sites['Co1'].adp_iso = 0.5
project.analysis.aliases.create(id='biso_Co1', param=structure.atom_sites['Co1'].adp_iso)
project.analysis.aliases.create(id='biso_Co2', param=structure.atom_sites['Co2'].adp_iso)
project.analysis.constraints.create(id='biso_Co2', expression='biso_Co2 = biso_Co1')
project.display.constraints()

project.analysis.fit()
project.display.fit.results()

edi fit: project cosio_d20, 1418 pts fitted / 1418 loaded, 39 free
   iter   time (s)   Rwp (%)  reduced χ²   change
                        4.05         4.64
      1      0.046      4.02         4.57   1.6% ↓
  done · converged · 1 iters · reduced χ² 4.57 · Rwp 4.02 % · 0.05 s

project.display.pattern('d20')

items.title: Oxygen occupancies
items.text:
Last, the oxygen occupancies, which change the intensities as the displacements do.

structure.atom_sites['O1'].occupancy.free = True
structure.atom_sites['O2'].occupancy.free = True
structure.atom_sites['O3'].occupancy.free = True

project.analysis.fit()
project.display.fit.results()

edi fit: project cosio_d20, 1418 pts fitted / 1418 loaded, 42 free
   iter   time (s)   Rwp (%)  reduced χ²   change
                        4.02         4.58
      1      0.043      3.97         4.45   2.7% ↓
  done · converged · 1 iters · reduced χ² 4.45 · Rwp 3.97 % · 0.05 s

project.display.pattern('d20')

project.display.pattern('d20', x_min=40, x_max=60)

project.display.fit.correlations()

project.display.structure('cosio')

items.title: Save the project
items.text:
project.save_as('cosio_d20')

Saving project to 'cosio_d20'

items.text: Google Colab Open in Google Colab Download Notebook

items.title: Co₂SiO₄ on D20 at 2.3 K
items.text:
Fit the magnetic structure of the olivine Co₂SiO₄ to constant-wavelength neutron powder data from D20 at ILL, measured at 2.3 K, below its ordering temperature. The cobalt moments order with k = 0 in the magnetic space group Pnma.1: Co1 may point in any direction, Co2 only along b.

The project is the catalogue case pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20_2k, the one the command line and the app's Examples open. Its two Co sites share one displacement, and the two FCJ asymmetry terms are tied, from the start.

import easydiffraction as edi

items.title: Load the project
items.text:
project_path = edi.download_data('pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20_2k', destination='data')
project = edi.Project.load(project_path)
structure = project.structures['cosio']
experiment = project.experiments['d20']
project.display.constraints()

Data 'pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20_2k' is at data/pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20_2k-773039d8ca78/pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20_2k

The project marks what its fit frees. The fit below frees it in stages, so start with all of it fixed.

for parameter in project.free_parameters:
    parameter.free = False

project.display.pattern('d20')

items.title: Perform the analysis
items.text: The nuclear structure comes first, in the usual order; the magnetic moments come last, once the nuclear peaks are fitted.

items.title: Scale, 2θ zero and cell
items.text:
experiment.linked_structures['cosio'].scale.free = True
experiment.instrument.calib_twotheta_offset.free = True
structure.cell.length_a.free = True
structure.cell.length_b.free = True
structure.cell.length_c.free = True

project.display.parameters.free()

project.analysis.fit()
project.display.fit.results()

With the peaks in place, the sixteen background points follow the level between them.

items.title: Peak widths
items.text:
experiment.peak.broad_gauss_u.free = True

items.title: Co₂SiO₄ on D20, cooling scan
items.text:
Fit the olivine Co₂SiO₄ with its magnetic structure to the whole D20 cooling scan, 213 patterns from 497.4 K down to 2.3 K, one after another and from the lowest temperature up. First the fit is staged on the 2.3 K pattern, the scan's template; then each later pattern starts from the previous result. The cobalt moments stay free at every temperature and fall towards zero near the Néel temperature, about 50 K.

The project is the catalogue case pd-neut-cwl_cosio-d20_scan-213f, the one the command line and the app's Examples open. Its two Co sites share one displacement from the start.

items.title: La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ on HRPT
items.text: This tutorial fits the cubic perovskite La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ to constant-wavelength neutron powder data measured on HRPT at PSI. It builds the structure by hand, loads the measured pattern from EasyDiffraction's collection, describes the experiment, links the two and fits them, showing the pattern and the parameters after each step. The other tutorials load their structures from a CIF.

items.title: Import the library
items.text: import easydiffraction as edi

items.title: Define the project
items.text:
A new project is empty: it holds no structure and no experiment until you add them.

project = edi.Project(name='lbco_hrpt')

items.title: Define the structure
items.text:
La and Ba share the corner site of the cubic cell, Co sits at its centre and O on the face centres, in space group P m -3 m. Every atom starts with an isotropic displacement of 0.5 Å².

project.structures.create(name='lbco')
structure = project.structures['lbco']
structure.space_group.name_h_m = 'P m -3 m'
structure.cell.length_a = 3.88

structure.atom_sites.create(
    id='La',
    type_symbol='La',
    fract_x=0,
    fract_y=0,
    fract_z=0,
    wyckoff_letter='a',
    occupancy=0.5,
    adp_iso=0.5,
)
structure.atom_sites.create(
    id='Ba',
    type_symbol='Ba',
    fract_x=0,
    fract_y=0,
    fract_z=0,
    wyckoff_letter='a',
    occupancy=0.5,
    adp_iso=0.5,
)
structure.atom_sites.create(
    id='Co',
    type_symbol='Co',
    fract_x=0.5,
    fract_y=0.5,
    fract_z=0.5,
    wyckoff_letter='b',
    adp_iso=0.5,
)
structure.atom_sites.create(
    id='O',
    type_symbol='O',
    fract_x=0,
    fract_y=0.5,
    fract_z=0.5,
    wyckoff_letter='c',
    adp_iso=0.5,
)

project.display.structure('lbco')

items.title: Define the experiment
items.text:
The measured pattern comes from EasyDiffraction's collection: 2θ, the counts and their standard uncertainties.

data_path = edi.download_data('pd-neut-cwl_lbco-hrpt-hrpt-data', destination='data')
project.experiments.add_from_data_path(
    name='hrpt',
    data_path=data_path,
    sample_form='powder',
    beam_mode='constant wavelength',
    radiation_probe='neutron',
    scattering_type='bragg',
)
experiment = project.experiments['hrpt']

Data 'pd-neut-cwl_lbco-hrpt-hrpt-data' is at data/pd-neut-cwl_lbco-hrpt-hrpt.xye

experiment.instrument.calib_twotheta_offset = 0.3
experiment.peak.broad_gauss_u = 0.08
experiment.peak.broad_gauss_v = -0.1
experiment.peak.broad_gauss_w = 0.1
experiment.peak.broad_lorentz_y = 0.08

A flat background of five points, and the two ends of the pattern left out of the fit.

for position in (10, 30, 50, 110, 165):

experiment.excluded_regions.create(start=0, end=5)
experiment.excluded_regions.create(start=165, end=180)

experiment.linked_structures.create(structure_id='lbco', scale=9)

project.analysis.aliases.create(id='biso_Ba', param=structure.atom_sites['Ba'].adp_iso)

items.title: Your own measured data
items.text:
Measured data can also come from a file on your own disk. add_from_data_path reads a file of time-of-flight, intensity and uncertainty columns into a new experiment, here in a project of its own; the experiment then needs its instrument, profile and linked structure, as above. The file here is SEPD's pattern from the collection, saved to disk first.

data_path = edi.download_data('pd-neut-tof_si-sepd-sepd-data', destination='data')
own = edi.Project(name='own_sepd')
own.experiments.add_from_data_path(
    name='mine',
    data_path=data_path,
    sample_form='powder',
    beam_mode='time-of-flight',
    radiation_probe='neutron',
)
own.display.pattern('mine')

items.title: Co₂SiO₄ sc-neut-cwl
items.text: Google Colab Open in Google Colab Download Notebook

items.title: Co₂SiO₄ on HEiDi
items.text:
Fit one Co₂SiO₄ crystal measured on HEiDi at MLZ at 300 K, 55 K and 2.5 K. Each temperature has its own structure and its own reflections, and the three are fitted independently: each fit sees only its own data and gives its own goodness of fit and uncertainties. At 2.5 K the cobalt moments order, and the magnetic structure is fitted too.

The data are those of Sazonov et al., Acta Cryst. B 64 (2008) 661-668. The 2.5 K file has no usable uncertainties, so they are estimated from the 55 K data of the same crystal (see the case's provenance); the fitted 2.5 K uncertainties depend on that estimate.

items.title: Import the library
items.text: import easydiffraction as edi

items.title: Define the project
items.text:
The independent fitting mode fits each experiment on its own, against the structure it links.

project = edi.Project(name='cosio_heidi')
project.analysis.fitting_mode = 'independent'

items.title: Define the structures
items.text:
Load the three structures from EasyDiffraction's collection, one per temperature. Each starts from the published positions with a small displacement tensor on every site. The 2.5 K structure also carries the magnetic space group Pnma.1 and the moment directions it allows, Co1 in any direction and Co2 along b, with every moment at zero. The files mark what the fit frees; the fit below frees it in stages, so start with all of it fixed.

path = edi.download_data('sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-cosio_300k', destination='data')
project.structures.add_from_cif_path(path)
path = edi.download_data('sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-cosio_55k', destination='data')
project.structures.add_from_cif_path(path)
path = edi.download_data('sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-cosio_2k5', destination='data')
project.structures.add_from_cif_path(path)
for parameter in project.free_parameters:
    parameter.free = False

Data 'sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-cosio_300k' is at data/sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-cosio_300k.edi
Data 'sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-cosio_55k' is at data/sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-cosio_55k.edi
Data 'sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-cosio_2k5' is at data/sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-cosio_2k5.edi

project.display.structure('cosio_2k5')

items.title: Define the experiments
items.text:
Load the reflections of each temperature and link each dataset to its structure. HEiDi's wavelength is 0.552 Å; the extinction is FullProf's anisotropic Larson model, with its six coefficients starting at zero.

data_paths = {
    '300k': edi.download_data('sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-heidi_300k-data', destination='data'),
    '55k': edi.download_data('sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-heidi_55k-data', destination='data'),
    '2k5': edi.download_data('sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-heidi_2k5-data', destination='data'),
}
for temperature, path in data_paths.items():
    project.experiments.add_from_data_path(
        name=f'heidi_{temperature}',
        data_path=path,
        sample_form='single crystal',
        beam_mode='constant wavelength',
        radiation_probe='neutron',
        scattering_type='bragg',
    )
    experiment = project.experiments[f'heidi_{temperature}']
    experiment.instrument.setup_wavelength = 0.552
    experiment.extinction.type = 'larson-anisotropic'
    experiment.linked_structures.create(structure_id=f'cosio_{temperature}', scale=10)

Data 'sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-heidi_300k-data' is at data/sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-heidi_300k.hkl
Data 'sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-heidi_55k-data' is at data/sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-heidi_55k.hkl
Data 'sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-heidi_2k5-data' is at data/sc-neut-cwl_cosio-heidi-heidi_2k5.hkl

Names for the three structures and experiments.

items.title: Foundations
items.text: EasyDiffraction calculates diffraction patterns from crystallographic models and fits selected model parameters against measured observations. It helps you connect a proposed structure with experimental evidence and retain the choices behind the result. This guide explains the model and workflow shared by every interface.

items.title: One product, several ways to work
items.text:
The application provides a visual workspace in a browser or on a desktop. Python supports scripts and notebooks. The command line runs analyses declared by saved projects. These interfaces use the same project model and current diffraction engine.

Choose the interface that fits your task. A complete saved project lets you continue the analysis through another interface without rebuilding its scientific inputs by hand. Setup, available controls and file-writing behaviour are described in the respective interface sections.

How you want to work Start here First fit Visually, in a browser or on your desktop EasyDiffraction graphical application Application Follow an example In a Python script or notebook EasyDiffraction in a Jupyter notebook Python Python Follow an example From a terminal or shell script EasyDiffraction command-line session Command line Follow an example

items.title: From a model to a result
items.text:
A structure describes the crystalline material. An experiment describes how its pattern is measured or simulated, including instrumental effects and background. The analysis joins them: calculate a prediction, select parameters that may vary, and fit against observations when those observations are available.

From measurement to analysis explains where this analysis sits after acquisition and reduction.

items.title: Follow the workflow
items.text:
Each stage has its own page; the analysis workflow follows a project from its inputs to an assessed result and a report.

  1. Project
  2. Structure
  3. Experiment
  4. Analysis
  5. Report

items.title: Start from a reproducible example
items.text:
An example project includes structures, experiments and starting conditions together. Use an example that matches your intended measurement, and read its provenance and reference comparison before treating it as a template for new work.

For your own analysis, keep the source of the structure and data, the experimental conditions, the fitting choices and the software version. A report tells others about the result; the saved project is what you reopen to continue.

items.title: Understand the physics
items.text: Physics explains diffraction, scattering, peak profiles, fitting equations and conventions behind the calculations. About covers the project, licensing, support and citation.

items.title: From measurement to analysis
items.text: EasyDiffraction compares a crystallographic model with diffraction measurements. Understanding where that comparison begins helps you choose suitable inputs and recognise what a fit can establish.

items.title: Acquisition, reduction and analysis
items.text:
1. Acquisition
  2. Reduction
  3. Analysis

items.title: Acquisition
items.text:
Record the detector response while the sample scatters the incident beam. This example uses a two-dimensional detector.

Beam, sample and detector: the three cones are the (100) and (001) magnetic and the (221) nuclear reflections of Co₂SiO₄ at λ = 1.87 Å Raw detector image, computed from the D20 pattern measured at 2.3 K

items.title: Reduction
items.text:
Apply the relevant corrections and turn detector measurements into observations with uncertainties. For powder diffraction, these are often a one-dimensional intensity profile.

Reduced diffraction pattern of Co₂SiO₄ at 2.3 K

items.title: Analysis
items.text:
Compare a calculated pattern with the observations, fit the model and inspect the result. EasyDiffraction focuses on this stage.

Measured, calculated and residual patterns of Co₂SiO₄ at 2.3 K Magnetic structure model of Co₂SiO₄ Illustration credits

Every figure on this page shows EasyDiffraction's Co₂SiO₄ example: neutron powder data at 2.3 K from D20 at the ILL. The instrument is drawn from that geometry; the raw detector image is computed from the measured pattern; the reduced pattern, the fitted pattern and the structure model are rendered by EasyDiffraction itself.

Keep the reduction history and experimental context with the project: they affect how uncertainties and agreement factors should be interpreted.

items.title: A model of the sample and the experiment
items.text:
The calculated intensity depends on more than atom positions. EasyDiffraction separates the model into two connected parts:

Part Describes Examples Structure The crystalline sample Unit cell, symmetry, atom sites, occupancies, displacement parameters Experiment How it is observed Wavelength or time-of-flight calibration, peak profile, background, scale and excluded regions

A disagreement between measured and calculated patterns can therefore have several causes. A peak-position error may come from the cell or calibration; a broad mismatch underneath peaks may come from the background; an intensity mismatch can involve the structure as well as experiment settings.

items.title: Calculation and fitting
items.text:
1. Structure + experiment
  2. Calculated pattern
  3. Compare with observations

A calculation predicts the diffraction pattern from the current structure and experiment. It does not need measured intensities. Use it to inspect peak positions and the influence of the model before fitting.

A fit needs observations to compare against. A least-squares fit reduces the weighted difference between observations and calculations: it changes the parameters marked as free, while fixed parameters still contribute to the calculated pattern. The starting model, free-parameter set, constraints, excluded regions and minimizer conditions all influence the result.

Start from a physically meaningful model. Inspect the initial pattern, allow parameters to vary deliberately, and review the result after each meaningful change. Adding more free parameters may reduce a residual without making the model more informative.

items.title: Least squares and Bayesian analysis
items.text:
Both compare a model with observations, but summarise parameter uncertainty differently.

Approach What it reports Least squares A best-fit parameter set and, when the covariance can be estimated, standard uncertainties and correlations Bayesian sampling A posterior distribution combining a likelihood with prior information, from which credible intervals and correlations can be summarised

The fitting instructions in this documentation use least squares. Its objective and covariance conventions explain the reported uncertainties. Bayesian sampling is a separate workflow; the older library's sampler choices should not be assumed to be available in this application.

items.title: Interpreting the result
items.text:
Convergence describes how the optimisation ended. It does not by itself establish that the sample model is correct or that all uncertainty sources have been captured.

Inspect the observed and calculated pattern, the residual, parameter uncertainties and correlations, and the physical plausibility of the result. Fit quality explains these checks in more detail.

items.title: The same ideas in every interface
items.text: The app makes these relationships visible. Python lets you express them in a script or notebook. The Command line runs the analysis already declared by a saved project. All use the same project model.

items.title: Data formats
items.text: EasyDiffraction keeps a saved analysis as an Edi project. It reads crystal structures and experiments from CIF, imports measured patterns from plain text, and exports reports as readable documents. Use the complete project to continue an analysis; use the other formats to bring data in or to share a result.

items.title: Edi and CIF
items.text:
Edi is EasyDiffraction's own format for saved project state, written with a .edi suffix. It uses CIF-like syntax — named data items, data blocks and loop_ tables. Most of its keys match the IUCr CIF names, and it adds EasyDiffraction-owned keys where no official CIF key is defined, which happens most often for experiment settings.

CIF (Crystallographic Information File) is the crystallographic exchange format maintained by the International Union of Crystallography. It is human-readable, and its dictionaries define the meaning of each name: coreCIF covers common crystallographic quantities, pdCIF covers powder diffraction, and magCIF covers magnetic structures. EasyDiffraction follows these names for CIF import and report output where they fit.

In short, Edi round-trips the whole project — structures, experiments, data, analysis settings and results — while CIF is the standard way to exchange a single crystal structure or to export a strict report. The Parameters section lists the Python path, Edi key and CIF key side by side.

items.title: In a project, only Edi
items.text:
A saved project contains only .edi files:

project/
├── project.edi
├── structures/
├── experiments/
├── analysis/
└── reports/

project.edi carries the project-level information; the other folders hold the structures, experiments and fitting settings, and the reports when you ask for them. The folder can be packaged as a .zip archive, and the app, Python and Command line all accept a project folder, its project.edi, or an archive.

You can still bring in data from other formats for convenience — a crystal structure or an experiment from CIF, and measured points from a text file — but EasyDiffraction writes everything back as .edi when it saves. If a folder holds both lbco.edi and lbco.cif, the .edi file is read and a warning names the .cif one, so a saved project never keeps CIF files.

Format What you use it for Edi project Reopen and continue the analysis with its structures, experiments, data, settings and results Structure from CIF or .edi Import one crystal structure into the project, for convenience Experiment from CIF or .edi Import one experiment with its settings and any stored data, for convenience Measured-pattern text file Supply observations to an experiment, for convenience HTML, PDF or CIF report Export a readable account of the analysis to share

A structure imported from CIF is a starting point. It still needs an experiment, instrument settings and measured data or a calculation range before it describes a complete analysis.

JSON suits structured data in programming, but for crystallographic data it is more verbose than the CIF-style layout:

items.title: Importing a CIF
items.text:
A CIF file can bring in a structure or an experiment wherever a .edi file can. EasyDiffraction reads both CIF 1.1 and CIF 2.0, and goes by the names inside the file rather than by its suffix.

  • A structure gives its cell, space group and atom sites, with their displacement parameters.
  • An experiment gives its type, instrument, peak profile, background, excluded regions, linked structures and measured points. An experiment added to a project must link structures the project already holds.

Imported values start fixed unless they carry a standard uncertainty: a value written as 3.8909(1) is read as free, while a bare 3.8909 is read as fixed. Free the remaining parameters you want to fit before fitting.

Every item in the file is either used, checked against what EasyDiffraction derives itself, reported as not read, or stops the import with an error that names it. Items that are not read come back as warnings beginning with crysta.schema.cif_items_not_read, each with a reason, so you can see exactly what was ignored.

A structure is read from the one block that gives a cell, and an experiment from the one block that gives experiment items and no cell. A file with several such blocks is refused. Magnetic and modulated structures and mmCIF files are not supported.

items.title: Structure files
items.text: A saved structure — .edi or CIF — adds one crystal structure to the current project. It imports the structure model only; it does not open a complete project. The Structure stage shows the file contents.

items.title: Experiment files
items.text: A saved experiment — .edi or CIF — adds one experiment with its measurement settings and any stored data. Check its linked structures after import. A measured-data text file such as .xye instead supplies observations to an existing experiment. The Experiment stage shows the file contents.

items.title: Measured-pattern text files
items.text:
Powder observations can be supplied as plain text columns for x, intensity, and optionally the standard uncertainty of the intensity:

  • For constant-wavelength data, x is 2θ in degrees.
  • For time-of-flight data, x is time of flight in microseconds.
  • A supplied uncertainty is used as the observation's standard uncertainty. Check it as carefully as the intensity.

After loading, the measured data are stored in the experiment's .edi file. The project keeps the source filename as context but does not depend on that original text file to reopen the stored measurement.

Check the imported pattern

Inspect the units, range, retained observations and any import messages. A readable file is not evidence that its columns or units describe the measurement you intended.

items.title: Observations and calculation ranges
items.text: A fit-ready experiment declares its observations and uncertainties; a simulation experiment declares a calculation range instead. A project may contain both kinds: calculation covers all of its experiments, while fitting uses those with observations.

items.title: Saving and sharing a project
items.text:
Hand on the complete project folder or archive to keep its saved model, embedded observations and analysis choices, and keep any external scan inputs as well. A report is a separate output, and saving a project does not create one automatically.

The exact file dialogs, import messages and write-back behaviour are interface-specific:

  • Application: measured-data import and saving projects.
  • Python: experiment input and project loading and saving.
  • Command line: accepted project inputs and output destinations.

See the shared Report stage for document formats and provenance.

items.title: Glossary
items.text: These terms are shared by the application, Python library and command line. The interface changes how you work with them, rather than changing their scientific meaning.

items.title: Project and model
items.text: Term Meaning Project The complete analysis: structures, experiments, data, analysis settings and saved results. A project can be kept as a folder or a .zip archive. Structure A crystallographic model of a phase, including its space group, unit cell and atom sites. Experiment The observation or simulation associated with an instrument model, profile, background and contributing structures. Parameter A model quantity such as a cell length, atom coordinate, scale or profile coefficient. Any such parameter may be free or fixed. Constraint A declared relationship that reduces independent freedom between model quantities. A tied value is not another independently fitted parameter.

items.title: Experiment types and labels
items.text:
These coloured labels mark the attributes of a measurement. They are generated from the experiment registry and shared by the app, the example catalogue and the guides.

An experiment combines one label from each family below. For example, the first fitting is pd neut cwl. Choose the measurement type before loading data; a listed attribute does not imply every combination is available.

items.title: Purpose
items.text: Label Meaning Fitting Compare a calculated model with measured intensities and fit its parameters. Simulation Calculate the pattern from the current model without measured intensities.

items.title: Fitting mode
items.text: Label Meaning Single Fit one experiment. Joint Fit several experiments together with shared model quantities. Sequential Fit a scan in order, using the preceding result as the next starting point. Independent Fit each dataset from the same starting model.

items.title: Sample form
items.text: Label Meaning pd Diffraction from many crystallite orientations, usually measured as an intensity profile. sc Diffraction from an oriented crystal, measured as individual reflection intensities.

items.title: Probe
items.text: Label Meaning neut Diffraction using neutrons; nuclear scattering and, where modelled, magnetic scattering contribute. xray Diffraction using X-rays; the scattering model depends on the electron distribution.

items.title: Beam mode
items.text: Label Meaning cwl A specified incident wavelength; powder patterns are commonly expressed against 2θ. tof Neutron wavelengths are separated by arrival time. Calibration relates flight time to diffraction geometry.

items.title: Scattering type
items.text: Label Meaning Bragg Model the crystalline contribution from lattice reflections.

items.title: Structure
items.text: Label Meaning Crystal Atoms, their positions and displacements in the unit cell. Magnetic A crystal structure whose magnetic atoms also carry moments, related by magnetic symmetry.

items.title: Interface
items.text: Label Meaning AI assistant An assistant such as ChatGPT or Claude sets up and fits the project from your request.

items.title: Analysis
items.text: Term Meaning Calculation or simulation Evaluation of the model with its present parameter values. A simulation may use a calculation range without measured observations. Fit Optimisation of the chosen free parameters against measured observations. Residual The difference between observed and calculated signal. Its pattern can reveal systematic disagreement that a single agreement factor hides. Standard uncertainty The uncertainty reported with an estimated parameter or observation. A fitted uncertainty reflects the assumptions of the fit, rather than every possible systematic error.

items.title: Patterns and crystallographic quantities
items.text: Term Meaning Reflection Diffraction associated with a set of lattice planes. A Bragg-position mark indicates where that reflection is expected in the pattern. Background The slowly varying contribution under diffraction peaks, represented by the background model chosen for the experiment. Unit cell The repeating geometry described by cell lengths and angles. Fractional coordinates A position expressed relative to the unit cell. Space group The crystallographic symmetry. Its setting identifies the coordinate convention used to describe that symmetry and the atom positions. Occupancy The occupation of an atom site. Atomic displacement parameters (ADPs) Displacement around an atom's average position. Isotropic and anisotropic representations use different parameters. Scale factor The weight of a structure's contribution to an experiment's calculated intensity. Its scientific interpretation depends on the experiment model and phase conventions.

items.title: Files and dictionaries
items.text: Term Meaning Edi (.edi) EasyDiffraction's saved project format. It uses readable CIF-like syntax with keys that describe the project model. CIF Crystallographic Information File, a scientific exchange format with dictionaries maintained by the IUCr. A structural CIF and a complete Edi project serve different purposes. coreCIF, pdCIF, magCIF Dictionaries of general crystallographic, powder-diffraction and magnetic-structure quantities. Edi project keys are EasyDiffraction's project names, mapped to these where one applies.

items.title: Online sources
items.text:
EasyDiffraction can load structures, experiments, measured data and whole projects from the web. Each place it reads from is an online source. Two are built in: the Crystallography Open Database (COD), for structures, and EasyDiffraction's own collection, which holds the examples and the tutorial data. You can add your own collection, for example your group's shared data.

The desktop application installs a copy of EasyDiffraction's collection with itself, so the examples and tutorials open without an internet connection. When the connection works, the application reads the online collection, which has the newest entries.

items.title: Use an online source
items.text:
• Application: on the Structure or Experiment page, open Load and choose From web…. Pick a source, search, and press Load on a row.
  • Python: edi.load_collection("https://example.org/my-data") reads a collection; edi.list_data() and edi.download_data("pd-neut-cwl_lbco-hrpt") list and download entries of EasyDiffraction's collection.
  • Command line: edi collection list, edi collection find ID and edi collection fetch ID, each with --source URL_OR_FOLDER for another collection.

items.title: Add your own source
items.text:
1. Open Preferences and the Projects tab.
  2. Under Online sources, press Add online source. A new row appears.
  3. Type a name and the collection's base URL: the address that holds its index.json.

Each source is one row of three lines: its name, what it holds and its URL.

The switch at the end of a row hides a source from From web… without removing it; the minus button removes a source you added. The two built-in sources can be switched off but not removed.

items.title: How a collection is laid out
items.text:
A collection is plain files behind one base URL, for example a GitHub repository or any static web server, with one index.json at the top:

index.json
structures/   structure files (CIF or .edi)
experiments/  experiment files (.edi)
data/         measured data (.xye, .dat, …)
projects/     whole projects, zipped

Only index.json is required to have that name and place; the folders are a convention. Every file the index lists is read from its path relative to the base URL.

items.title: The index format
items.text:
index.json is an object with two keys: "schema": "edi-data-index/1" and "entries", a list. Each entry describes one thing to load:

Field Required Meaning id yes A name unique in the collection, used to find and download the entry kind yes structure, experiment, data or project files yes One or more files, each with path (relative to the base URL) and format; sha256 and bytes are checked when given name, description no What the search results show formula, elements no The chemical formula in Hill notation and its element symbols, for searching space_group, cell no The space group and the six cell parameters of a structure radiation, technique, instrument, facility no How an experiment or its data was measured source no Who provides the entry

A file path is made of folder and file names (letters, digits, ., _, ~ and -) joined by /, never starting with / or containing ... A download whose size or digest differs from the index is refused.
