items.title: Parameters
items.text:
Parameters describe both the sample and the experiment. Changing a cell length moves calculated reflections; changing a scale changes their contribution to intensity; changing a background coefficient changes the signal underneath the peaks.

Look up GUI labels, Edi keys, Python paths and CIF names. The tables below lead to a description of every category and field.

items.title: A value and its context
items.text:
A parameter's value needs its name, units and place in the model to be meaningful. Typical groups include:

Group Examples What to check Unit cell Lengths and angles Units, symmetry and plausible geometry Atom sites Fractional coordinates and occupancies Site meaning, symmetry restrictions and composition Displacements Isotropic or anisotropic displacement parameters Convention, units and physical interpretation Instrument and profile Calibration shifts and peak-width terms Instrument geometry and profile definition Background and scale Background points or terms, phase scales Baseline behaviour and how phases contribute

The project model keeps structure quantities separate from experiment quantities. They may still be correlated in a fit.

items.title: Free and fixed
items.text:
A free parameter is allowed to change during fitting. An active fixed parameter contributes to the calculation but keeps the value you supplied. A stored-only field is different: retaining it does not establish a calculation effect. The parameter index identifies the known stored-only fields and model-specific roles.

Review the free set before fitting. Only quantities that can vary independently belong in it. A fit cannot vary a value that describes the setup, such as the crystal radius, one that symmetry or a constraint sets, one the fit's data cannot determine, such as a cell fitted only to single-crystal intensities, or one the calculation has no derivative for yet. A value saved as free that cannot be fitted is loaded as fixed, with a message saying so. Keep the chosen free set with the saved project. Edit the free set in the Application or Python Python. Command line uses the choices saved in the project.

items.title: Uncertainties
items.text:
A fitted parameter may have a standard uncertainty. Interpret it together with the measurement uncertainties, the model and correlations with other parameters.

A small standard uncertainty describes precision under the fit's assumptions. It does not remove uncertainty from calibration, sample effects, missing phases, an unsuitable background, or another systematic source.

See fit quality for how parameter uncertainties relate to agreement factors and the residual.

items.title: Constraints and symmetry
items.text:
Some values are related by the crystallographic symmetry; others may be linked by a declared constraint. Such values are not independent fitting directions.

For example, a symmetry restriction on a coordinate cannot be treated as an arbitrary free coordinate simply because a table displays it. The application disables the free checkbox on such a value. Inspect the relationship before interpreting how many independently variable quantities the fit has.

items.title: Bounds and starting values
items.text:
Use meaningful starting values. A fit begins at the project's current parameter values, and its final state can depend on that starting point.

Model-admissibility limits describe which values the model accepts. They have a different purpose from an optimiser's search bounds. Check the applicable model and interface documentation before treating a displayed range as an editable fitting interval.

When interpreting a constrained or limited value, check the applicable model and fitting settings. A result reaching a permitted limit can be a reason to inspect the starting assumptions, observations and parameter correlations.

For scan analyses, the fitting mode determines whether each dataset starts from the same template values or from the previous fit.

items.title: Names in code and files
items.text: A parameter can have a Python access path, an Edi persistence key, and a scientific CIF report name. These have different jobs. Use the current Python documentation for code and data formats for saved files. The code access path and the saved-file key need not be identical.

items.title: Parameter names across interfaces
items.text:
Compare names used in the app, saved Edi projects, Python and CIF. Select a parameter to read its meaning, units and model restrictions.

About these names

GUI names use the application icon patterns. Python paths are checked against the supplied examples; use .value or .free on a parameter. CIF mappings can include EasyDiffraction extensions. A dash means no declared mapping was found; a listed field is not necessarily editable or independently free in every model.

items.title: AI assistant
items.text:
EasyDiffraction is ready for AI assistants. The desktop app has an assistant built in, which works in your open project. ChatGPT or Claude, in their desktop apps or command-line tools, can write a notebook or a project for you from your own files: a structure and a measured pattern become a fit set up in stages, which you then run, check and change.

Where Built-in assistant Your own assistant Notes Desktop app The built-in assistant is an optional part of the desktop app and needs a ChatGPT account. Web app The browser has no built-in assistant; open the project your own assistant writes. Python Your own assistant writes a Jupyter notebook ready to run. Command line Your own assistant writes a project ready for edi fit.

items.title: Built-in assistant (desktop app)
items.text:
The desktop app's assistant can explain a fit, suggest which parameters to fit next, and carry out supported actions in your open project. The Fit with the AI assistant tutorial follows one run.

Answer, and the assistant fits the structure

The assistant after it fitted La₀.₅Ba₀.₅CoO₃ on HRPT (the tutorial).

items.title: Install and connect
items.text:
1. Select AI assistant in the desktop installer. To add it to an existing installation, open Preferences → Updates → Open Maintenance Tool and add AI assistant, then restart the application.
  2. Open a project workflow page and select the robot button in the toolbar.
  3. Select Connect ChatGPT and complete the OpenAI sign-in if prompted. The assistant needs an internet connection and a ChatGPT account with access to a compatible Codex model.

The assistant uses your ChatGPT plan’s Codex allowance. Model access and usage limits depend on the plan and workspace settings. OpenAI offers limited Codex access on some free accounts. Your account’s model access determines whether you need a paid subscription. OpenAI plans and usage limits

In the web app the robot button opens a note about the desktop app instead: the browser has no built-in assistant.

items.title: Work with your project
items.text:
Ask a question about the open project or describe the result you want. For example, ask which parameters to fit first and why, or ask the assistant to fit the background and inspect the residual before fitting the peak profile.

When EasyDiffraction asks for approval to share project information or attached files, review the selection before continuing. Use Stop to interrupt ongoing work.

Inspect the resulting pattern and fitted parameters before relying on the result. The fit quality guide explains how to assess a fit.

items.title: Show actions
items.text: Show actions, in the chat's composer, shows each action the assistant takes in the app as it works, on the control it uses. Off, the assistant works in the background and reports in the chat.

items.title: Your own assistant
items.text:
ChatGPT or Claude, in their desktop apps or command-line tools, can write what each interface uses, given the documentation, the tutorials and your files:

  • a Jupyter notebook ready to run: the Python AI assistant tutorial;
  • a project to fit with edi fit: the Command line AI assistant tutorial;
  • a project to open in the desktop or web app, as an alternative to the built-in assistant or in its place: the same Command line prompt.

Open a project it returns in the app:

Desktop app Web app

On Project, choose Open project…, then Folder and select the project folder. You can also drop the folder or its project.edi file onto the window.

On Project, choose Open project…, then Folder, or zip the project folder first and choose Zip archive. Where the project is kept afterwards depends on the browser; see Open and save files.

items.title: Analysis workflow
items.text:
A complete EasyDiffraction analysis connects the model of a sample with an experiment and keeps the decisions that produced the result. Follow these stages in any interface.

  1. Project
  2. Structure
  3. Experiment
  4. Analysis
  5. Report
Stage Scientific task Ready to continue when… Project Organise the analysis, inputs and provenance You can identify the measurement, model and starting conditions Structure Describe the crystalline phase or phases Symmetry, cell and atom sites represent your intended sample model Experiment Describe the observations and how they are calculated Data or a simulation range, instrument, profile, background and structure links are consistent Analysis Calculate, fit and assess The result has been inspected against the observations and physical model Report Communicate and retain the result The report matches the saved model and the complete project is retained

items.title: Choose how to carry it out
items.text:
Interface What its section provides Application Workspace, imports, parameter controls, fit progress and visual inspection Python Python Project objects, parameter access, analysis calls and result objects Command line Commands for saved projects, output options and automation

The scientific explanations belong here; the interface pages link back to them as needed.

items.title: Analysis
items.text: Analysis evaluates the combined structure and experiment model. A calculation predicts its pattern at the current values. Fitting changes selected independent parameters to improve agreement with measured observations.

items.title: Calculate the starting model
items.text:
Inspect the initial prediction before fitting. Check peak positions, widths, relative intensities and background against the measurement. A forward calculation can also explore a simulation with no observed data.

EasyDiffraction uses the crysta diffraction engine. The Physics section explains the models and conventions behind its calculations.

items.title: Select the independent parameters
items.text:
Choose which parameters may vary and which stay fixed. Respect symmetry and declared constraints. The fit begins from the current parameter values, so retain the starting state when comparing different fits.

Fit a set that the observations can constrain. Strongly correlated quantities can trade off against each other, improving an agreement factor while leaving the scientific interpretation uncertain.

items.title: How a fit iterates
items.text:
A fit is an iterative loop. A minimizer repeats these steps, adjusting the free parameters each cycle to reduce the weighted difference between the calculated and measured pattern:

  1. Set parameter values
  2. Calculate pattern
  3. Compare with data

The loop stops when the change falls below the convergence tolerance, or when the iteration budget is reached. Those limits are minimizer conditions, not part of the scientific model.

items.title: Fitting modes
items.text:
A fitting mode sets how your observations share a model: fit one experiment, several jointly, or a scan sequentially or independently. The mode is part of the project, so the app, Python and Command line run the same declared analysis.

Mode Use it for How the analysis runs single One experiment or the shown dataset of a scan Fits that experiment's observations joint Several experiments describing a connected model Fits their observations together sequential A scan whose neighbouring datasets should carry a starting model forward Fits datasets in order, seeding each from the preceding result independent A scan whose datasets should share the same starting point Fits every dataset from the template's starting values

A calculation without observations is a different action: it evaluates the model over a declared range and does not optimise against measured data.

items.title: Single and joint fits
items.text:
Start with a single fit when learning an example or checking one measured pattern. Inspect the initial calculation, choose free parameters, then fit and review the residual and agreement factors.

A joint fit brings several experiments into one optimisation, with complementary information about the same structural model. Check which parameters are shared and which belong to individual experiments: a good result in one experiment can hide poor agreement in another, so inspect each experiment's pattern as well as the combined result.

items.title: Sequential and independent scans
items.text:
A scan is a series of measured datasets, often recorded while temperature or another condition changes. It uses a template experiment and a declared set of files. In sequential mode, each result becomes the starting model for the next dataset — useful when the sample evolves gradually, though an unsuitable fit can influence the next starting point. In independent mode, every dataset starts from the same template values, keeping the starting conditions consistent while each dataset still needs an adequate initial model. Both modes fit files serially; their distinction is the starting state, not parallel execution.

Inspect convergence and failures for individual datasets, then compare fitted patterns and parameter evolution. A smooth trend alone does not prove that every dataset was fitted adequately. Keep completed results tied to the template and conditions that produced them, since changes to a template can make earlier results out of date.

items.title: Retain minimizer conditions
items.text:
The project records the descent strategy, convergence tolerance and iteration budget. These conditions govern how a run proceeds and when it stops; they are separate from the scientific model and its free-parameter choices.

The current project format declares them in the _minimizer category of analysis/analysis.edi. Use the current interface instructions for access.

items.title: Assess the fit
items.text: Judge a fit using the pattern, the residual, the fitted parameters and the agreement factors together. A successful optimisation is the beginning of that assessment, not the end.

items.title: Inspect the pattern and residual
items.text:
Compare the measured and calculated intensities over the full range, then inspect individual peaks and regions that disagree.

  • Are peak positions aligned?
  • Do widths and shapes agree across the range?
  • Does the model account for the observed peaks?
  • Is the baseline appropriate between and under peaks?
  • Does the residual contain a repeated or systematic pattern?
What you see Check first Learn more Peaks shifted across the pattern Cell, wavelength and instrument calibration Cell and symmetry, calibration Widths or tails disagree Profile function and its coefficients Peak profiles Baseline follows the residual Background model and excluded regions Background Extra measured peaks Missing phases, impurities or measurement artefacts Structure model Unstable values or large uncertainties Free parameters, bounds and correlations Minimization

Reflection marks show where the structures predict Bragg positions. They help connect a profile disagreement to the contributing phases, but they do not explain every source of intensity.

items.title: Read the agreement factors
items.text:
Rp and Rwp summarise the powder-profile mismatch. Rexp and reduced χ² connect that mismatch with the observation uncertainties and independent parameter count. The fitting and statistics chapter gives their equations and conventions.

A small R factor is only part of the assessment

There is no universal R-factor threshold that makes every model acceptable. Data range, exclusions, uncertainty estimates, background and the model affect the values. Inspect the curve, residual and physical parameters together.

items.title: Check parameters and correlations
items.text: Inspect whether the result makes physical sense. Review free parameters, their uncertainties, correlations and any values that have reached their bounds. Strong correlations can mean that several parameter combinations explain similar changes in the observations, so treat individual uncertainties with care. Changing the data range or constraints changes the question the fit answers.

items.title: Distinguish termination from correctness
items.text: Reaching an iteration limit is different from satisfying a convergence condition. A converged fit may still describe an unsuitable structure or an incorrect instrument setting. Keep the starting model and minimizer conditions with the result so another person can repeat the same optimisation.

items.title: Compare results fairly
items.text:
Fitting measured data tests how well the chosen model describes that measurement. Comparing a calculation with an independent reference program checks the implementation for that model and case. Both are useful; neither replaces inspection of the physical result. A meaningful comparison between programs needs matching observations, structures, background, profile, excluded regions, free parameters and starting conditions.

Single-crystal examples fit reflection observations rather than a powder profile; read their example-specific references instead of applying powder-profile factors without checking the observation model.

items.title: Run the analysis
items.text:
• Application: free-parameter controls and fitting, mode selection and scan controls.
  • Python: calculation, fitting and result objects.
  • Command line: calculation and fit commands.

items.title: Experiment
items.text: An experiment describes an observation of the sample or a simulation of that observation. It combines measured data or a calculation range with an instrument model, peak profile, background and links to the contributing structures.

items.title: Identify the measurement
items.text:
Choose the sample form, radiation probe and beam mode that match the experiment. Constant-wavelength powder data use scattering angle; time-of-flight data use the calibrated time axis. Single-crystal observations describe reflections rather than a continuous powder profile.

The glossary explains the experiment labels. Use the checked example catalogue to find an appropriate starting model and its stated scope.

items.title: Observations or a simulation range
items.text:
Measured observations supply the intensities and uncertainties used by a fit. A simulation supplies the range over which the current model is calculated, without requiring measured intensities.

A saved experiment declares one of these forms. A complete project can contain both simulation and measured-data experiments; fitting uses the experiments with observations.

For powder text input, verify the independent variable, its units, intensity and optional uncertainty column. Check the imported range and any import diagnostics. See data formats before preparing a file.

items.title: Instrument and peak profile
items.text:
Instrument settings describe the measurement geometry and calibration, such as wavelength or the relationship between time of flight and diffraction spacing. The peak profile describes reflection shapes and broadening.

Check peak positions and widths before changing structural parameters to compensate for disagreement. A profile appropriate to one instrument or measurement need not describe another.

items.title: Background and excluded regions
items.text:
The background accounts for the contribution beneath the diffraction peaks. Select a representation appropriate to the measurement and inspect its behaviour between and under peaks. An automatic estimate is a starting model that still needs inspection.

Excluded intervals remove observations from the fitting objective. Record why a region is excluded; an exclusion changes the evidence used to assess the model and its agreement factors.

items.title: Contributing structures and scales
items.text:
Link each contributing structure and review its scale. One experiment can sum contributions from several phases. Several experiments can observe the same structure under different measurement conditions.

Scales connect phase contributions to the experiment. Interpret any derived composition or phase fraction in the context of the model and its conventions.

items.title: An experiment file
items.text:
An experiment is saved as one .edi data block. The example below is experiments/cu_ka.edi from the LiF project — a constant-wavelength X-ray simulation, so it declares a calculation range (_data_range) rather than measured points:

data_cu_ka

_experiment_type.sample_form powder
_experiment_type.beam_mode "constant wavelength"
_experiment_type.radiation_probe xray

_scattering_source.xray_form_factor it1992
_scattering_source.xray_dispersion sasaki1989

_instrument.setup_wavelength 1.54056

A measured experiment instead carries a background definition and a loop_ of measured points with their uncertainties. See data formats.

Configure experiments in the Application or Python Python, then use the saved experiments from Command line.

items.title: Project
items.text: A project is the complete working record of an analysis. It keeps structures, experiments, data, fitting settings and saved results together, so the analysis can be inspected, repeated and continued.

items.title: Establish the analysis
items.text:
Start from an included example, open an existing complete project, or assemble the inputs for a new measurement. Give the analysis a useful identity and retain the provenance of its structural model and observations.

A structural CIF supplies a structure. An experiment CIF supplies an experiment, including its measured points, and a measured-pattern file supplies observations. Neither alone describes a complete analysis: the project connects them with instrument settings, structural links and analysis choices.

items.title: What belongs together
items.text:
Part Role Structures Sample models, including symmetry, cell and atom sites Experiments Measured observations or simulation ranges, instrument/profile/background settings and links to structures Analysis Free parameters, constraints, fitting mode and minimizer conditions Results and reports Recorded outcomes and documents for inspection and sharing

Several experiments can share a structure while keeping different measurement settings. Several structures can contribute to one experiment. Check those links explicitly when adding phases or measurements.

items.title: Keep a complete copy
items.text:
The project folder contains project.edi and associated structures/, experiments/, analysis/ and reports/ content. A .zip archive packages the folder for transfer. See data formats.

A constant-wavelength X-ray powder example is laid out like this:

lif_xray/
├── project.edi            project metadata and display settings
├── structures/
│   └── lif.edi            LiF structure model
├── experiments/
│   └── cu_ka.edi          measured or simulated experiment
├── analysis/
│   └── analysis.edi       fitting mode and minimizer settings
└── reports/               generated documents (when requested)

Only project.edi exists right after you create a project; the other folders appear as you add structures, experiments and analysis settings. project.edi records the project-level metadata and display choices:

_edi.schema_version 3

_metadata.name        lif_xray
_metadata.title       "LiF [Fm-3m] · Calculated example"
_metadata.description "Cu Kα₁ calculated profile · X-ray scattering factors and dispersion"

The Structure and Experiment pages show the contents of lif.edi and the experiment file.

Keep the full folder or archive when moving between interfaces. Retain starting conditions separately when you want to compare them with a fitted state. Saving a report is separate from saving the editable project.

items.title: Check completeness
items.text:
A runnable experiment needs valid structure links and either observations with uncertainties or a calculation range. The complete-project reader rejects ambiguous or incomplete saved inputs instead of returning a partially loaded project.

For scans, retain the declared source files and their order along with the template and results. Moving a project may require checking that the scan's external input location is still available.

Create, open and save a project in the Application, Python Python or Command line.

items.title: Report
items.text: A report brings the model and analysis outcome into a document for inspection and sharing. It complements the complete project, which retains the editable analysis.

items.title: What to retain
items.text:
A useful scientific account identifies the structures, experiments, observations, analysis choices and outcome. Inspect the fitted values, uncertainties and agreement factors together with the observed/calculated patterns and residuals.

Report settings select optional material such as charts, correlations, reflection information, data points and scan evolution. Include what the reader needs to assess the result, and retain the complete project when a report omits large data tables.

items.title: Choose an output
items.text:
Output Purpose Current interface support Interactive HTML Share a readable document with interactive figures Application, Python and Command line Offline HTML Embed chart libraries so the document can be opened without fetching them Application, Python and Command line PDF Share a paginated document with static figures Application CIF report Exchange a scientific account of structures, experiments and results Application, Python and Command line

A structural CIF used as input and a CIF report serve different purposes. Neither replaces the complete project; see data formats.

items.title: Save the model and the report
items.text:
Saving a project and writing its report are separate actions. A model or report-settings change can make a previously saved report out of date. A file that has been removed can be marked missing.

Check report state before sharing it. Keep the report together with the matching project, measured data provenance and software version. For a scan, include the template, file order and information about failed or incomplete results.

items.title: Generate the document
items.text:
• Application: Report page, export formats and saved-state indicators.
  • Python: report rendering and save methods.
  • Command line: report output and freshness checks.

See How to cite when preparing a publication or handing an analysis to a collaborator.

items.title: Structure
items.text: A structure describes a crystalline phase used to calculate diffraction. It combines a symmetry setting, unit-cell geometry and atom sites. It can be imported from a structural CIF or assembled from crystallographic information.

items.title: Symmetry and setting
items.text:
The space group and its setting determine which positions and cell parameters are independent. Check that the chosen setting matches the coordinate system of the structural data you are using.

A symmetry-related value is not an additional independent fitting direction. A table can display several coordinates or cell dimensions even when symmetry relates or fixes them. Symmetry is one of several reasons a fit cannot vary a value; see free and fixed.

items.title: Unit cell
items.text: Cell lengths and angles define the repeating geometry. Their units and allowed relationships depend on the crystallographic setting. Inspect the starting calculated reflection positions before fitting the cell: an instrumental calibration error can also move peaks.

items.title: Atom sites
items.text:
Quantity Meaning What to inspect Site label and element Identify the site and its scattering species Consistency with the intended composition Fractional coordinates Locate the representative site in the unit cell Coordinate setting, symmetry and plausible geometry Occupancy Describes occupation of the site Composition and relationships between species sharing a site Displacement parameters Describe displacement around the average position Isotropic/anisotropic convention, units and physically meaningful values Wyckoff position Describes the site's symmetry position Restrictions on coordinates and site multiplicity

Keep the displacement convention used by the source structure; quantities expressed with different conventions should not be compared by name alone. Use parameters for free/fixed values, uncertainty and constraints.

items.title: Phases and experiment links
items.text:
A project may contain several structures. An experiment links the structures that contribute to its calculated pattern, with a scale for each link. Adding a structure to the project does not by itself establish that it contributes to every measurement.

Check which phases should contribute and whether their links are enabled. Structural quantities describe the sample; background and peak-profile terms belong to the experiment even though they also affect the calculated pattern.

Edit structures in the Application or Python Python, then calculate the saved model from Command line.

items.title: Understand the reference
items.text:
An example may compare a calculated curve or fitted values with FullProf or another reference. Read what is being compared: identical model settings, a program-specific model, or a labelled regression result answer different questions.

Use fit quality to interpret agreement factors. The references validate the paths and cases they cover; they do not establish every possible model or interface operation.
